speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one or two general observations. We found ourselves in a position of happy unanimity on this bill, in the committee. I think this is a case where all concerned-the banks, who were originally the sole parties mentioned as affected by the guarantee, the credit unions who came and presented their case to the committee, and all others concerned-came to a common conclusion which seemed most likely to benefit the industry.
I should like to add just a word more. The appearance of representatives of the credit unions from both the east and west coasts was a matter of great interest. The story they had to tell, of the way they had stepped in and assisted the industry, the history of their success, and their readiness to co-operate in the extensions proposed by the bill, all seemed to augur well for the success of the bill. And, as I say, we found ourselves in a position of happy unanimity in recommending the amendment we now have before this committee for consideration.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Definitions.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before clause 2 carries I should like to join in what the hon. member for Greenwood has just said. I was not a member of the banking and commerce committee, but some of us were invited to sit in as representatives from fishing communities.
I listened to the discussions. It is true that all members of the committee were very much impressed by the presentation brought forward by the credit unions from the east coast, from Quebec and from British Columbia. I think this was a rather unusual situation. This was a bill which, undoubtedly, had received careful consideration by the government before it was introduced,

Fisheries
and one which involved a pretty complicated question of financial administration. After having studied the measure, in view of the representations made by the credit unions the committee unanimously accepted a very important amendment, which we are glad to see is now approved and accepted by the government. I think this speaks very well for the credit unions. It would seem to indicate the greatest possible display of co-operation on their part, and of co-operation from all parties in the House of Commons. Because, as someone said at the close of that committee meeting, we sometimes think we are in four parties when we sit in the House of Commons; but this time we had no parties, because it was entirely a matter of unanimity. It is a great tribute to these credit unions, because it is well known that for a period of 20 years they made possible the financing of the operations of fishermen when no one else would do it. When I say this I am not criticizing the banks in any way, because probably in many instances the risks were such that the banks could not be expected to accept the responsibility; and there was also the further fact that in so many communities there are no banks.
It was these little credit unions which came into the picture and, over a period of years, helped not only to rehabilitate the fishing industry but also to strengthen themselves and also to increase their stature to such an extent that they were recognized unanimously by all members in the committee, and now by the government of Canada.
This is a step in the right direction. We hope the bill will be amplified still more in the future. But at least this is a great step in the right direction. It is one of several steps which have been taken during the last few years when we have had various matters of legislation dealing with the fishing industry. At one time it looked as if the fishing industry was the forgotten industry in Canada. Ministers who were dealing with that department felt, it seemed, that they were either on the way up or on the way out. It is good now to see that the industry is getting the recognition it deserves.
I notice in section 2 that the definition of "fisherman" is one "whose principal occupation is participation in a primary fishing enterprise". I hope the minister will-and I am sure he will-use quite a bit of latitude in the interpretation of that expression, because certainly on the east coast, while there are many fishermen whose full time occupation is that of fishing, there are others

who spend part of their time in farming or other occupations and fish for only part of the year.
The income tax branch of the Department of National Revenue have had some difficulty in specifying what is a "principal" occupation, and it is possible that the minister in this instance may have the same difficulty. In this connection, again, I hope and expect that he will give those who are engaged in fishing the benefit of any doubt he may have. It may be that there will be some who would be spending no more than six months in a year in fishing operations; yet, if they are bona fide fishermen for part of the year, they should come under this section.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to associate myself with other hon. members who have spoken, in recording my approval of the action taken by the committee on banking and commerce in recommending the inclusion of credit unions, and my appreciation of the fact that the government has accepted this recommendation.
I think this was a striking indication of the capacity of two young men who appeared before the banking and commerce committee, one of these from Nova Scotia and the other from British Columbia. They gave most helpful accounts of the operations of credit unions, and impressed every member of the committee with their competence to represent their organizations.
It was, I think, almost amazing to see the committee gradually realizing that it was unanimous. Those of us who spoke first of all in support of the inclusion of credit unions-and I speak for myself in this regard -got up feeling that we had certain opposition to overcome. When we began to look for it, to our surprise we found there was no opposition, and that everyone was in accord with the move.
As I say, those two young men, Mr. MacMullin from Nova Scotia, and Mr. Mc-Master from British Columbia, deserve the thanks of the co-operative movement in this country. May I conclude by saying that this group as a whole records its very great satisfaction on the new status that has now been accorded to the co-operative banking system of this country.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Before this clause carries I should like to raise one point, already discussed by my colleague from Digby-Anna-polis-Kings. I am referring to the expression "principal occupation" as it appears in the clause. Is it clear that that is going to be interpreted by and large so that no question will arise? If not, might it not be worth

while to consider adding the word "substantially". If we get to the stage where we have to say that it is a man's principal occupation, it seems to me there may be some difficulty. Whether it is necessary to leave it or not, I ask the minister if he would consider it now, because the word "substantially" would get away from the difficulty if it would be sufficiently strong for the purposes of the minister. I should like him to consider it even now.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext: This actual phrasing was the phrasing of our department. It is the phrasing which is satisfactory to the fishing industry. After all, it is not the government who says that this man can qualify for a loan and this man cannot; it is the judgment of the bank manager or the chairman or the treasurer of the credit union who is going to approve the application for a loan made to the fishermen. He can very quickly tell from the actual amount of income the fisherman reports he makes from his fishing whether the fishing is the principal or substantial part of his income. But the actual phrasing of this section is satisfactory to the fishermen's organizations, to the credit unions, and to the Department of Fisheries.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext: I think the situation will work out exactly as the minister has described it, subject only to this. Would it be possible in terms of common sense for the department to raise the question that loans were unauthorized because they were made to people whose principal business was not fishing? Is the minister satisfied?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it was by accident that I was the first speaker at the resolution stage who brought to the attention of the minister the advisability of considering the inclusion of credit unions as well as banks in this legislation. I was pleased to note the support which that suggestion received at the time and subsequently in the committee on banking and commerce. I am delighted to see the amendment which the committee recommended. Having said that, I want to record my pleasure at the amendments which have been recommended. I know that this is a recognition of the excellent work which has been done over the years in financing fishermen.
I have been a bit concerned over the matter brought up by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings with regard to the interpretation of the words "whose principal occupation is participation in a primary fishing enterprise". I too hope that a generous interpretation will be given to that statement. For instance, I note that in my riding there are a good many people who actually fish only two months. They are lobster fishermen and they are limited to two months' activities because of the season. Yet they spend much of the rest of the time preparing for the short fishing season. They consider their primary occupation as being that of fishermen, although they may be employed for a greater length of time during each year at some other subsidiary occupation and may earn even a greater amount of money from the subsidiary activity than they earn from fishing activities if they happen to have a bad year with a good deal of stormy weather during the fishing season. I should therefore

Fisheries
like to think that the interpretation put on this legislation would mean that it would apply to persons who are fishermen within the meaning of the term "fishermen" in that area.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
I should like to commend the government for introducing this legislation, to thank the committee for introducing the amendment to include the credit union as a lending agency, and also to express my gratitude to the government for accepting the amendment and incorporating it in the present bill.
The matter of credit is one of the greatest problems that have been connected with the fisheries of Newfoundland and is, I believe, one factor which has contributed greatly to the slowness of its development. In Newfoundland the fisherman gets credit from the local supplier. The local supplier in turn gets credit from a larger supplier, perhaps in the same neighbourhood. This larger supplier in turn gets credit from the general supplier at St. John's who in turn gets credit from the banks. As will be seen, there are at least two and sometimes three middlemen distributing credit between the bank and the fishermen themselves. This bill which will enable the fisherman to get credit directly from the bank will, I believe, be a great stimulus to the fishermen to modernize their equipment. It can be seen that when there are so many middlemen between the bank and the fishermen, the cost of this credit must necessarily be high and be a burden to the fishermen themselves.
With respect to the inclusion of the credit unions, I may say that in Newfoundland by law we call them co-operative credit societies, but they are the same thing. In my riding there are 262 settlements. All of them are fishing settlements. These 262 settlements are distributed along a coast line of, roughly,
1,000	miles. In that area there are only four communities in which banks are located and three of those banks are within a radius of 30 miles of each other. The other bank is located at the extreme end of the riding. It can be seen that if the lending institutions were limited to banks alone, this legislation would not be of a great deal of use to the fishermen of my riding. The fact that credit unions have been included will be a great blessing, although not at the very moment because at the present time there are in my riding few credit unions that are capable of lending amounts of considerable size. But I should like to point out that in my riding there are some 30 or 40 fishermen's locals of the Newfoundland fishermen's federation and each of those locals is capable of developing into a co-operative credit society. I hope

that the introduction of this legislation will stimulate that development.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to support the amendment. At the same time I wish to express thanks on behalf of the New Brunswick members to the government and to the members of the banking and commerce committee for their acceptance of this amendment. I am sure it is going to mean a great deal to the fishermen in financing equipment and other fishing gear. As you know, most fishermen- particularly inshore fishermen-who use small boats and small equipment and live in remote villages have little source of credit. A credit union is their only banking institution. Again I express the thanks of the fishermen, the credit unions and the cooperative societies to the government for their consideration and, I trust, acceptance of this amendment. In particular I wish to express the thanks of the fishermen, the credit unions and the co-operative societies of Northumber-land-Miramichi.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3 as amended-Minister to pay losses of hanks under certain conditions.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
I should like to make one brief reference to clause 3. Like other members who have spoken, I am happy to see the amendments which have been proposed in the definition section but I think that clause 3 indicates what was suggested at the resolution stage, namely that this being a new piece of legislation, it is still somewhat in an experimental stage. In that connection I would mention the limitation which is placed on the size of the loan, that of $4,000, in clause 3 of the bill. At this time I am not rising to object to the fact that that has been the figure set. However, I hope that the ministers, and in particular the Minister of Fisheries, will be making a close study of the workings of this bill and that it will not be too long before we shall find coming into the house an amendment to the bill which will relax some of the provisions with regard to the maximum size of loan. I think the Minister of Fisheries would probably agree with me that on the British Columbia coast, because of the type of fishing boats and gear which is being developed there and which is coming into increasing use, there may be cases where loans of a larger size than the present maximum of $4,000 could be quite usefully used by the fishermen. As I say, I hope that matter will be kept under constant study and that perhaps within the next session or two we shall find coming into the house an amendment

Fisheries
which will have the effect of increasing the maximum allowable under the insured loans plan.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Hon. members should bear in mind the fact that the purpose of this bill is to provide for intermediate credit. As far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, fishermen can get long-term credit. For loans for the acquisition of new boats and their permanent capital equipment there are provincial loan boards. In case of draggers and long-liners there is also a subsidy from our department. There is no such provincial fisheries loan act on the west coast in British Columbia, but it is easier there to get longterm loans from other sources.
As far as the $4,000 limit is concerned, I feel that is a reasonable start for the type of fishermen we are trying to help, namely the small fishermen. Our fishermen's indemnity fund provides insurance on equipment up to $7,500, on which there is a 60 per cent coverage, which means that the fisherman would get back $4,500 on his policy in event of loss. This guarantee ties in very closely with the $4,000 limit on these loans. But the main purpose of this is to grant intermediate credit to enable a man to improve his boat, his engine or his gear, and not so much for the acquisition of new capital equipment which is a matter of long-term loans and is dealt with by other agencies.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 4 and 5 agreed to.
On clause 6-Extent of minister's liability.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEE ON LOANS TO FISHERMEN
speechtext:
It is on clause 6 that an amendment is to be moved by the government. While I am on my feet I should like to say one or two things about the bill. Various members have rightly given credit to the credit unions for having this legislation amended. I think the real credit goes to the members of parliament from the fishing ridings. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said that the way this developed was quite an unusual occurrence. After all, the bill is patterned on the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and since there is no provision for credit unions in the Farm Improvement Loans Act the officials of the Department of Finance, I am quite sure, took it for granted they would not be included here. But on the night the resolution was discussed, fishing members from every corner of the house got up and spoke so strongly in favour of credit unions that the Prime Minister, as you may remember, called me over and told me to send the bill to the banking and commerce committee so that we could see whether they could be included.
Therefore it was the pleas of members from fishing ridings that brought about this amendment.
Clause 6 was drafted at a time when only the banks were included in subclause (b) which provided that the total amount of loans which would be guaranteed in the next three years would be $15 million. Now that credit unions are to be included the subclause has been reworded to provide a $10 million guarantee in the total of loans to the banks and $10 million to the credit unions. The actual amendment reads:
(b) to make any payment
(i)	to a bank in respect of loss sustained by it as a result of a guaranteed loan made after the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed loans made by all banks exceeds $10 million, or
(ii)	to any lender in respect of loss sustained by it as a result of a guaranteed loan made after the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed loans made by all such lenders exceeds S10 million.
That is the exact wording of the recommendation that was made by the banking and commerce committee.

I do not know that I can make the statement the hon. member expected me to make, but I will repeat what I said the other day when the bill was introduced. The purpose of the bill is to declare that the seaway authority is a corporation empowered to take or use land without the consent of the owner within the meaning of section 35 of the Indian Act. If one refers to the Indian Act, one finds in subsection 1 of section 35 the following:
Where by an act of the parliament of Canada or a provincial legislature Her Majesty in right of a province, a municipal or local authority or a corporation is empowered to take or to use lands or any interest therein without the consent of the owner, the power may, with the consent of the governor in council and subject to any terms that may be prescribed by the governor in council, be exercised in relation to lands in a reserve or any interest therein.
I understand that there was thought to be some doubt as to whether the St. Lawrence seaway authority was, in fact, the kind of corporation that is described in subsection 1

of section 35 of the Indian Act. The purpose of this bill is merely to make it abundantly clear that the authority is that kind of corporation, and therefore has the power to expropriate lands in an Indian reserve. As hon. members know, in particular there are lands in the neighbourhood of Cornwall that form part of an Indian reserve and likewise there are also lands near Caughnawaga, in the province of Quebec, where the seaway authority will need to expropriate for the purposes of the seaway.

Certainly I think that all of us in the house, all of us on this side I am sure, would not want to do anything to delay or to hold up in any way the progress of the seaway itself which has been a dream of many Canadians, if not all Canadians, since the turn of this century. I was interested, in looking into the background of this bill, to find that even back in 1932 the Bennett government negotiated a treaty with the United States which died in the United States Senate. Both before and after that time, all parties had made very strenuous efforts to bring this seaway about.
I shall not, for many obvious reasons, touch on the broader aspects of the seaway. I think perhaps we will deal with some of those when
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act we come to the transport department estimates. I do think, in connection with this bill itself, we might pay attention for a moment to the attitude of the seaway authority to the responsibility with which it has been charged, and to its relationships with other groups. I feel that is important because we must read the bill in the light of the use which is going to be made of the powers which are being confirmed by this bill.
In that connection, I turn to certain observations of the president of the seaway, who will presumably direct measures under this amending act. He made a statement to the Montreal chamber of commerce, and in the course of those remarks he said this:	I will
read them first in the original French of which, while certainly not as good French as Mr. Chevrier used, it may be said "It is a poor thing, but my own." He said:
(Translation):
Other critics claim that our plans for remodelling Jacques Cartier, Victoria and Mercier bridges are inadequate. If this criticism bears only on the problem of traffic between both shores, I am not overconcerned about it. If it refers to navigation, I beg to differ sharply. This criticism is unjustified. Our statute, in effect, calls for canalization works, not for works having to do with roads or vehicular traffic. The St. Lawrence seaway authoriy was not established to solve traffic problems either at Montreal, at Beauharnois or at Welland.

I should like to rise on a point of order. What we are talking about at the present time is a bill which will enable the St. Lawrence authority to expropriate Indian lands. Now, I cannot offhand think of anything more remote from the bill than the Victoria bridge, the Jacques Cartier bridge or the Mercier bridge. It seems to me they are wholly irrelevant to the matter under discussion. We are not talking about the authority that has been given to the seaway authority under the statutes. We are not discussing its present powers of expropriation. All we are dealing with is the question of whether or not the seaway authority should be permitted to expropriate Indian lands.
Now, as the hon. member who is speaking knows, none of these bridges are located on Indian land. No expropriation of Indian lands is required in connection with the Mercier bridge, the Jacques Cartier bridge or the Victoria bridge. It is not, Mr. Chairman, as if there were not other opportunities for the hon. member to make these observations. There are estimates provided for the St. Lawrence seaway authority and when those are before the committee these remarks would be relevant.

St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR EXPROPRIATION OF INDIAN LANDS
speechtext:
In
connection with the minister's remarks, I might perhaps proceed in a few moments to discuss the bridges per se, at which time we can debate that. But it was my intention at this point, in setting the stage for my remarks, to point out that the seaway authority has had a callous disregard for the interests of those communities and those areas which are affected by their projects, and that in the light of that callous disregard which is evidenced in their own words, we should be doubly careful about giving them powers to expropriate lands from people who perhaps might not be in the same position as other people in this country to protect their own interests.
Now, turning again to my argument which, as I said, has nothing whatever to do with the bridges, I have here a news item from the Montreal Star of Tuesday, March 22, commenting on the speech of Mr. Chevrier, the president of the seaway authority, which says:
The head of the St. Lawrence seaway authority asserted today that it "has not been set up to solve problems of traffic either at Montreal, at Beauharnois or at Welland."
Hon. Lionel Chevrier, in an address to the Chambre de Commerce de Montreal, struck back at critics of seaway plans, whose views, he said, "are unjustified".
He said there were some critics "who pretend that our plans for remodelling Jacques-Cartier, Victoria and Mercier bridges are inadequate".
And this is the pertinent sentence:
"If this criticism takes note only of the problem of traffic between the two shores, I am not overconcerned."
And again, quoting Mr. Chevrier:
"Our statute, in effect, imposes on us the task of canalizing-not roadworks or traffic."
Here is a case in which we are being asked to confirm strong powers to be exercised by this authority, powers which they say they need for the completion of their job. These are powers, as I shall demonstrate in a few moments, which could redound greatly to the detriment of the Caughnawaga Indian reserve, and the Indians who live there. I think it is only right that, in examining this confirmation of powers, we should realize the way in which such powers are likely to be exercised. They are likely to be exercised, Mr. Chairman-and the quotations in both English and French which I have placed on the record substantiate this contention-in a way which says:	There
is only one thing which matters, and that is the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. Other interests, other desires, other people's feelings are not to be taken into consideration. They are-as Mr. Chevrier put it so well-"canalizing", and they

are going to drive the St. Lawrence seaway through, no matter who suffers in the process.
Now, in the course of following through on that very strong-minded and somewhat dictatorial attitude, the authority has established a route which requires them to expropriate these Indian properties. I now turn to a subject which, while the minister may not like it, has a direct relationship to the expropriation of these Indian lands which is the route of the seaway. There are, and were, numerous alternative routes in that area which the seaway could have followed. I suggest that the necessity for this measure coming before the House of Commons today would not have existed had the seaway authority taken a little more time and given a little more consideration to alternative routes.
We find for example that it is not only the Indian reserves which are troubled by the route chosen; it is causing problems also along that south shore of the river which could have been avoided, had a route more to the centre of the river been chosen.
Referring to that problem, we find an expert on the subject, Mr. George Mooney, of the St. Lawrence municipal bureau in Montreal, saying in a recent report:
One fact dominates the other. It is that, for all time to come, consequent upon the construction of the seaway channel in the location decided upon, a servitude has been placed on the St. Lawrence river which, hereafter, will necessitate costlier bridges or costlier tunnels than otherwise would be necessary had the channel been constructed more towards the mid-stream of the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR EXPROPRIATION OF INDIAN LANDS
speechtext:
Let
me turn now to the specific clause of the bill, Mr. Chairman. It would seem to me that this is primarily a rather cozy little arrangement which might leave the Indians very much out in the cold after negotiations between the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, his department and the St. Lawrence seaway authority. Section 35 of the Indian Act was read to us by the minister. He did not read subsection 3. I shall read it:
Whenever the governor in council has consented to the exercise by a province, authority or corporation of the powers referred to in subsection (1), the governor in council may, in lieu of the province, authority or corporation taking or using the lands without the consent of the owner, authorize a transfer or grant of such lands to the province, authority or corporation, subject to any terms that may be prescribed by the governor in council.
Section 35 goes on to state that any amount that is agreed upon or awarded shall be paid to the Receiver General of Canada for the use and benefit of the particular band of Indians. We have here a situation that

St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act is not comparable with that which I would say is normally envisioned by the act. The St. Lawrence seaway-and I made reference to this in my earlier remarks-is one of the great projects of this century. It is one which is affecting the economic life of both the immediate area through which it passes and a large section on either side. This is particularly so in so far as land values are concerned in the Montreal area. Without detailing farm by farm what is happening in that area, it is well to know that from Sorel up to and beyond the Caughnawaga reserve-and I use this as an example because I know the area perhaps a little better than I do the Cornwall area-on the south shore of the river land has skyrocketed in value. If there ever were gold-plated farms in the Dominion of Canada-and I hope the minister does not object to the terminology "Dominion of Canada"-these gold-plated farms exist in that area right now. Land is being transferred from owner to owner at prices which are unbelievably high, prices which, until this route was determined upon, would never even have been dreamed of or considered. The reason is that the Laprairie basin, which is immediately adjacent to the east of the Caughnawaga Indian reserve, is considered one of the areas likely to be the most highly developed industrially as a result of this seaway. In referring to that, Mr. Mooney, in a speech to the Engineering Institute of Canada, had this to say:
Now that the channel Is definitely under construction. a lively interest is being shown in the whole of the area abutting on the Laprairie basin. This vast area is being thought of as an ideal site for future industrial growth and development.
There is much common sense in this view. Large industrial sites with both port and railway facilities on the island of Montreal have now been virtually pre-empted. There are still areas where light and medium industry can be located but very little indeed which has the facilities which a large industrial operation requiring portside as well as railway sidings can function from. Any industry dependent on large shipments of primary natural resources such as coal, grain, iron ore, timber, petroleum, and other bulk commodities and whose output is destined for foreign as well as inland domestic markets requires both water and rail shipping facilities on its doorstep. Such sites are difficult to find on the island of Montreal today.
Referring to the value of this area, Mr. Mooney said:
It is for this reason that the Laprairie basin offers such promise and it is the existence, proximity and availability of the Laprairie basin and its hinterland that underlines the promise of future industrial growth and expansion in the Montreal area.
Here is an area which is immediately adjacent to one of these Indian reserves on which the seaway authority proposes to expropriate land. Similar things could be said about the


Cornwall area. Yet what protection, what means of assurance is there that these Indians will be getting a fair value for lands which may be expropriated? As far as I can see, unless the minister has some suggestion to offer, the bill presently before us gives no protection whatever.
It is a measure by which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, on the one hand, without any immediate interest in this save as one of his many responsibilities, that of looking after Indian affairs, works out an agreement with the St. Lawrence seaway authority which has a great interest in keeping the price down. It would seem to me quite possible that under such circumstances the people who would come out, not second but third or fourth or fifth place, would be the bands of Indians on this particular reserve. As I said before, the reason I am raising this point is that I do not think the section was originally written into the Indian Act envisaging the expropriation of lands under circumstances such as these.

speechtext: We might just as well settle that once and for all. I did not mention the St. Lawrence seaway authority, but I did say that the power of expropriation and administration under section 35 was designed to permit the expropriation of land by public utilities.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR EXPROPRIATION OF INDIAN LANDS
speechtext:
I
thank the minister for his interjection, but as all of us know there are various kinds of public utilities and there are various ways in which they influence the area in which they are erected. It is specifically my suggestion here that the normal public utility does not result in an increase in the value of land to anything like the magnitude which has resulted from the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. Normally a public utility like a water or power plant or something of that nature will spread its benefits almost equally for many hundreds of miles in every direction. The increase in the value of land close to such a public utility is not noticeably greater than the increase in the value of land three, four, five or ten miles removed from it.
Here we have a particular situation where land for many miles on either side of the seaway has grown tremendously in value, but where the land immediately adjacent to the seaway has increased in value to an almost incalculable degree. We are being asked to give the government power to turn some of that land over to the St. Lawrence seaway

authority without any particular qualification or any particular indication that the interests of the Indians concerned are going to be particularly well represented in a particular situation. That is the point of my criticism of this measure.
I would have been happy, and I think we all would have been happy, realizing that these lands must be expropriated if the government is going ahead with this project, and I think it would have been fairer to the Indians, had an agreement been worked out or had a measure been brought down in which there would have been arrangements for independent representation of the interest of the Indians and in some measure representation by the Indians themselves. I suggest that the business of one branch of the government negotiating with another branch of the government for an exceptionally valuable property, which neither of them own as such and which is essentially the property of people who were here long before even this long-lived government, is something which is not advisable.
To use the legal term, I should like to see the transaction at arm's length; I should like to see this a transaction in which two people do not have their hands in the same pocket, in which two people do not come to a conclusion which may be beneficial to them but which definitely will be a detriment to the people who are now rightfully in possession of the property being bartered for.
Having said that, I only add that I hope the minister can give us some assurance in this regard. We do not want to stand in the way of progress as represented by the seaway. Section 35 contains several references to terms that can be prescribed by the governor in council and before this measure passes I should like to have the minister give us some indication that those terms will include special protection for this group of people because of the special circumstances which surround the expropriations prompted by this measure.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR EXPROPRIATION OF INDIAN LANDS
speechtext:
I am very happy to give that assurance. I may say regarding the Caughnawaga reserve that negotiation between the St. Lawrence seaway and the band council have already begun. I do not know whether these negotiations are at arm's length, but they have been of a most friendly character. May I say that I regard it as my duty as superintendent general of Indian affairs to see that the Indians are just as well treated in these expropriations as anyone else. If I have any doubt on that score, or if they express any doubt on that score that doubt will be settled in the manner in

speechtext: Now that the minister of Indian affairs has just had a word to say -I may say I did not hear the previous discussion in connection with this matter- I should like to ask him this question. I wish the minister would clarify that matter. I think that is one of the major rights that the Indian tribes rely upon, namely that in treaties that have been entered into as between their respective Britannic majesties and the ancestors of the present Indians, those rights are above parliament. That has been the contention of the Indian tribes across this country and it is one of the things upon which they place the greatest reliance. I simply ask the minister this question. Has there ever been a case wherein the crown has been able, by procedures such as this or by a statute passed by parliament, to challenge and to deny those rights which were granted to the ancestors of

Indians living today on these reserves or on Indian lands and thereby taking from them the one possession they have, namely the right to rely upon a promise made to their ancestors that as long as the sun will shine and the rivers flow the rights granted by respective British sovereigns in direct treaty relations with the Indians should not be interfered with?

Mr. Speaker, when this measure was at the resolution stage I pointed out that our task of increasing salaries, pleasant as it is, must be regarded with a sense of responsibility. I further reminded the committee that many taxpayers who find their own incomes in process of reduction and not increase will inevitably look with a critical eye at salary increases; especially in those cases where the present salaries appear to them to be on a generous scale.
In studying the matter further, it seems clear that the salaries at present paid are on a reasonably generous scale and, indeed, to the ordinary taxpayer might look quite large. Further, we feel that salary increases should not be dealt with in any routine manner at the present time, particularly in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is budgeting for a deficit and there is still a good deal of unemployment. In these circumstances it seems fair to suggest that, when we consider increasing salaries already reasonably high in the judgment of most persons, we should have in mind at least three tests: First of all, length of service; second, extent of responsibility borne; and, third, recognized success.
Applying these to the tax appeal board and the tariff board-the transport board will be dealt with later-highly as we regard the services of both these bodies, and our regard is very high, we feel that the argument for increases does not seem conclusive or adequate except in the case of the chairman of the tariff board, Mr. McKinnon, who we

believe qualifies under all three tests and who has frequently represented Canada abroad with great distinction. As I said, I am confining my remarks to the tax appeal board and the tariff board. The board of transport commissioners will be dealt with separately. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we do not feel we can vote for the bill.

Mr. Speaker, as two or three of us in this group indicated when we were at the resolution stage, we feel that parliament should not be asked to support this legislation. I indicated at that time, as did my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), that in our view this legislation should be looked at in the same manner in which we looked at the legislation increasing the salaries of judges. We indicated in that case that we did not mind increases for those whose salaries were in what might be called the lower or medium brackets. But when we are dealing with salaries that are already well in excess of $10,000 a year, we do not feel present conditions warrant an increase.
As I indicated at the resolution stage, increases have been provided for all the positions covered by this bill, except one, within the last four years. In the case of the income tax appeal board, increases were provided for all the members in 1953. In the case of the members of the board of transport commissioners, increases were provided in 1951. In the case of the tariff board increases were provided for all but the chairman in 1953. We are dealing here, Mr. Speaker, with salaries which at the present time range from a low, if one can use that word, of $11,000 a year to a high of $16,000 a year. The proposed increases vary in themselves from $1,500 a year to $2,500 a year. We in this group are not opposed to efforts to improve the standard of living of our Canadian people. But we do think, as was pointed out so effectively by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway last Thursday, that this is not the place to start. We feel the place to start is with those whose standard of living needs to be increased.
If the government would come along at this session, as there is yet time to do, with some improvement in the position of those on old age pensions; if it had done better than it did with respect to those on the war veterans allowance or if it would consider the case of Canadian National retired employees or its own superannuated civil servants, there might then be some case for
Public Service
the government pleading for increases for the people mentioned in this legislation. Because that is our view, Mr. Speaker, we feel that we cannot support this measure.
I am interested in learning that the Progressive Conservatives have come to that view as well. It is true that at the resolution stage members of that party asked questions which led some of us to wonder whether they might support this bill. We are glad to have their support of our opposition to this measure. I must confess that we wonder why it is they were prepared to support the increases in judges' salaries, some of whom were already drawing much more than these people are drawing, but now take a different line. They approved of salary increases for judges already drawing $20,000 and $25,000 a year, yet now they feel that these salaries are too high. I leave that to the members of that party to explain. Mr. Speaker, in this instance, as so often happens, most of the points in argument were brought out at the resolution stage. However, one or two observations were made by hon. members, including myself, which might be amplified.
When the resolution was under consideration we made certain reservations and asked for more information. I do not feel, therefore, that there is any obligation resting upon us to support the measure from that standpoint.
In recent years this party has established its position of being against increases generally. We have been most wary of them, and have been consistent at all times, even though at times our stand may not have been the popular one. I find it amusing to review the anomalous position of the C.C.F. when they refer to the position this party has taken. In 1951 when we were debating a resolution respecting increased salaries for the board of transport commissioners that measure was given support by the C.C.F. Today, however, we find them saying that they are going to vote against the measure now before us. In addition to that they criticize what they say is an inconsistent position taken by this party, and say that when we oppose the measure we place ourselves in an unfortunate position.
The observations I made at the resolution stage were directed chiefly to the board of transport commissioners, and my thoughts today are along similar lines. I might add however that the same argument would have equal weight when applied to any of the requests for increases now set before us.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) spoke earlier in the debate there were two points of which he took cognizance. I think his words were that there were two sets of operations. It was pointed out first of all that these increases follow logically the increases in judges' salaries. I believe it will take only a moment to show that this is not true. Hon. members on the opposition and government sides of the house, when discussing increases in judges' salaries, pointed out that there were weaknesses in appointments to the bench and that satisfactory candidates were not available. It was indicated further that the Turgeon report had recommended a strengthening of the bench.
In addition, it was said by those taking part in the debate that, in the matter of appointments to the bench, different parts of the country have to be considered and that in different areas the duties are performed in greater or lesser degrees. It was said that
in some parts of the country the duties falling upon the judges were heavier than upon the judges in other parts. Except in the case of the chief commissioner, I suggest that none of these arguments can be applied in the present instance. The statement that the salary increases suggested in this instance follow logically the increases in judges' salaries, which found support in the House of Commons a short time ago, is not a valid argument.
The second point is a troublesome one, and concerns the civil servant status of members of these boards. The minister pointed out that there is a widening gap between the $2,500 increase given by statute to the chief commissioner and the smaller increases suggested for the rest of the members of the board.
This whole situation requires closer examination, and more by way of explanation. It is suggested that if the commissioners, other than the chief commissioner, are to be placed in the category of civil servants, they should be put in a special classification and should not be attached in any way to the chief commissioner or to other members of the judiciary. It is pointed out that the commissioners are non-professional, and the point is made that there are some lawyers serving on the commission-and I am referring particularly to the board of transport commissioners, of which two members are laymen. In view of this fact it is urged that these members are in the class of civil servants. I do suggest however that they are not in the same position as career civil servants, and the argument that senior civil servants were given increases in salary last year is not valid. These gentlemen are appointed to their positions later in their lives; they do not have the civil service background, as such, and perhaps in this respect they should be placed in the category of board members, where their positions would correspond to those of members of the pension commission, or some other body of that kind. We have always made the general reservation in connection with salary increases, that when salaries get above the $10,000 mark-the sum equalling the indemnity of members of parliament-very special consideration should be given. I suggest there is a danger that with these increases we would be establishing a spiral that would be hard to overcome.
On the one hand we must consider the increases that were made in the salaries of members of the bench. It is true that support for those increases was given, on our part, chiefly because of the necessity to strengthen the bench, as well as for some

other considerations. But to attach the salaries of members of the board of transport commissioners to the salaries of members of the bench, itself, is a dangerous procedure, because it means that every time the bench is brought into focus we are bound automatically to consider salaries of members of the board of transport commissioners. I suggest this creates a vicious spiral, because every time civil servants receive increases we would have to decide automatically that the board of transport commissioners must receive the same treatment.
So that we must consider this as a triangle, with the bench on one side, permanent civil servants on the second side, and the board of transport commissioners on the third. Each time one is affected, all are aifected. This is a danger, and I suggest a separation should be made so that each could be dealt with on its merits.
I have pointed out the two considerations in this instance, and have said that the increases now sought do not fall into the same category as those voted to members of the bench a short time ago. Any such submission must fail, because those who introduced the bill with respect to judges' salaries have not followed the same line of argument. The second point, which is even more dangerous, is that we should place them in a special category of the civil service. I have pointed out that the members of these boards are not in the same position as permanent civil servants; and the fact that last year highly placed civil servants received increases in salaries does not mean that those set out in this measure should be made.
The three tests suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) earlier in the debate are to my mind the most valid that could be applied in this instance. I suggest there should be a complete reconsideration of the suggested increase in salaries to members of the board of transport commissioners, other than the chief commissioner who is, perhaps, in the same position as appointees to the bench, and whose salary is fixed by statute.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the transport board is not weak. They have done a very good job. We have fine men on that board but because they are doing a good job, are strong and are taking their onerous duties to heart, it does seem strange that we cannot support the salary increases. This is one time when virtue does not have its own reward. If they were in the position of the bench itself, which has weaknesses which we all admit, then perhaps we could make out a good case; but I do feel that we
Public Service
cannot support the increases at this time because it would be inconsistent with our position throughout the past few years, particularly in 1951, when we said that a spiral of increases for everybody under present economic conditions in Canada would be dangerous.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose the increases that Bill No. 507 proposes. As a basis of my remarks, I am going to use five headlines that appeared on the market page of the London Free Press of last Thursday. The first one is: "Farm Status in Economy Seen Falling". The second: "Textile Company Gives Up, Blames Government Policy." This company had been in operation for 32 years in St. Catharines, Ontario, and had employed 432 people.
The dominion bureau of statistics issued a report last week which said: "Cash Farm Income Drops." This was the third successive annual drop. There was a fall-off of $34,200,000 in the first three months of 1955. Then we have an item from the steel companies which reads: "Steel Firms Worried on Price, Wages Rise." And finally: "Spokesmen for Industry Fear Idling of 5,000." This refers to the footwear industry in Canada.
The fact that during the past year many thousands of Canadians have found their incomes or salaries drastically reduced, some of them experiencing a reduction over a period of three years and, as far as agriculture is concerned, no relief in sight, should be an indication that this is not the time to indulge in a further round of increases. It is only an invitation to all groups in the economy that can do it to force another price rise, another wage rise or another salary increase. Because of that I am taking this opportunity to oppose it.
I am not going to deal with the question of the increase that was granted to the judges. My colleague the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) dealt with that very well. I do not think I need to answer the accusations of the C.C.F. party prior to the lunch hour; but I do want to point out that this is another round of salary, wage and price rises. Do not forget that we have already priced ourselves out of world markets. The article in the Free Press dealing with the footwear industry points out that the daily wage paid to the workers in foreign lands amounts to 44 cents to 75 cents per day, while our Canadian workmen receive $1.45 an hour. We cannot afford to increase prices in the face of such competition.
I oppose this bill because thousands of working people would accept the proposed

increase as a full yearly wage. Thousands and thousands of people in Canada would be glad to take it as a full yearly wage. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this bill merits more discussion than was indicated in the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) this morning. He seems to treat these increases in salaries in a rather light-hearted manner. There would seem to be a rather touching concern for those high-paid appointees of the government. Let us have a look at the figures. The chairman of the board of transport commissioners is to be raised from $16,000 to $18,500; the assistant chairman from $14,000 to $15,500; the deputy chairman from $13,000 to $14,500 and the other commissioners from $12,000 to $13,500. The other two boards, the income tax appeal board and the tariff board, are to get similar increases. The ordinary members of each of these two boards are being raised to a yearly salary of $13,500.
These are not small salaries, Mr. Speaker. These men will be among the highest paid people in the country. It is not a matter of raising the salaries because of an increase in the cost of living. There is not the slightest suggestion of that. Of course, were the government to lose the increases on that fact the argument would be completely untenable. This is in fact merely a handout to

government appointees who are already receiving very high salaries.
I suggest that the minister has given no valid reason whatever for these increases. His explanations will be found in the first place on page 5171 of Hansard for June 23, where he had this to say:
The decision to increase the salaries of the members of the various boards follows logically upon the decision to increase the salaries of the judges. It is for the purpose of carrying out a decision which was made consequent upon the other decision.
These men with whom we are now dealing are not in the same category as judges at all. The judges are dealing with the general public. These particular men occupy special positions in government. As the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) has pointed out this afternoon, there is no fairness in tying together the salaries of the judges and the salaries of the men who occupy positions on these boards. But then the minister gave a second reason which is to be found at page 5176 of Hansard. It also was given on June 23. He said this:
The fact is that when the proposed changes are carried out the salaries of the junior members of the board-that is the members-will be at the rate of that of an assistant deputy minister . . .
He summed up his reasons in these words:
You therefore really have the two forces operating. You have the judges' salaries in the one case and you have the senior civil servants' salaries in the other. We have attempted to place those in their proper relation to other circumstances.
He was questioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) concerning tying in the salaries of the members of these boards with those of assistant deputy ministers, and the minister admitted that the figures in this bill are being assimilated to the highest salary being paid to an assistant deputy minister.
I have taken the trouble to look up the salaries that are being paid to assistant deputy ministers and I find that the situation is as follows. In the Department of Agriculture the assistant deputy minister gets $9,500 a year as compared with $12,000 which the ordinary member of the board of transport commissioners is already getting and the $13,500 he will get if this bill becomes law. In the defence department there are two assistant deputy ministers, one paid $12,000 a year and one at $9,500. In the defence production department, there is one at $13,500. That is one case in which an assistant deputy minister is getting the figure that these members of the board will be getting when the bill becomes law. One only gets $12,000. In the Department of External Affairs there are one at $11,000, two at $9,750 and one

at $9,625. In the Department of Finance there are two at $15,000 and one at $13,500; they receive the highest pay of any assistant deputy ministers. In the Department of Fisheries there is one assistant deputy minister at from $9,000 to $10,000. In the Department of Justice there are two at $15,000 and one at $9,000. In the Department of Labour there is one at from $9,000 to $10,000. In the Department of National Revenue there are two at $10,500. In the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources there are two at $11,000. In the Department of Public Works there is one at $11,000. In the Department of the Secretary of State there is one at $10,500. In the Department of Trade and Commerce there is one at $10,500. In the Department of Veterans Affairs there is one at $12,000 and in the Department of Transport there is one at $12,000. I point out that only in the three departments-those of finance, justice and defence production-are assistant deputy ministers getting the salaries which will be paid to the ordinary members of these boards.
I think it is particularly significant that the assistant deputy minister of transport is getting only $12,000. The members of the board of transport commissioners do not have any more important work to do than does the assistant deputy minister of the Department of Transport; yet they are to get $1,500 a year more than he gets. Furthermore, the deputy minister of transport gets only $15,000 a year but the chairman of the board of transport commissioners is now to get $18,500 and the assistant chairman is to get $15,500 which is $500 more than the deputy minister of transport; and the deputy chief commissioner is to get $14,500 which is only $500 less than the amount paid to the deputy minister of transport.
We believe that these salaries are out of line. I do not understand why the government would, for example, increase the salaries of the board of transport commissioners in view of the stand that board has taken with respect to railway labour in Canada. Just a year ago-on February 15, 1954 -the board of transport commissioners handed down a decision on the application of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for an increase in freight rates. If that course had been followed and if a central authority of that kind had been set up, there might have been some excuse for these increases. Before this clause carries, there is just one further word I should like to say. It applies not only to this clause but to all of them. Indeed, it applies to all increases of this kind that have been proposed from time to time by the government. It has been argued repeatedly that higher salaries are needed in order to attract to these positions the calibre of persons desired to do this kind of work. It seems to me that there is a fallacy in that argument of which note should be taken.
As I see it, all that means is that in order to attract a person who is already making $30,000 or $40,000 a year you have to offer a salary which approaches the amount he is already making. The point that my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and others of us in this group have tried to make from time to time is that calibre is not necessarily determined by the amount of salary a person may be making. A lawyer

may be making $30,000 or $40,000. This, of course, proves he is a very smart lawyer but it may not prove he is of the calibre that it is desired to have in judicial positions. It may simply prove he knows the tricks of the law. It may simply prove he knows how to get around the law. It does not necessarily follow that the calibre of person needed in a judicial position, whether it is as chairman or a member of one of these boards or whether it is on the bench, can be determined by the amount of money involved.
It seems to me that this parliament has not yet given due weight to the opportunity for public service that is involved in positions of this kind, to the prestige that goes with them and to the measure of security involved. In moving an amendment to Bill No. 192 on June 15, I thought I was moving a very simple amendment in which the qualifications the Canadian library association has set would be the qualifications that would be recognized in making appointments to the positions of parliamentary librarian and assistant librarian. However, the amendment seems to have produced a reaction that may or may not be significant. The minister expressed himself immediately as very forcibly opposed to this amendment. It would almost seem as if he had already some person or persons in mind for these library posts, persons who did not meet the qualifications this amendment suggests.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration introduced the bill with bland assurance and said that this was his bill only by courtesy. Later he said the bill was the result of the work of the joint committee on the library, and there was no need whatever for politics.

When I said it was a very simple amendment suggesting the qualifications recognized by the Canadian library association, politics suddenly reared its confounded head. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre pointed out, red herrings were dragged all over the debate. The minister said that this bill was recommended by the joint library committee, and that is why it was his bill by courtesy. However, the hon. member for Peterborough pointed out that the committee had not drafted the bill and, as I understand it, had not even seen it before it was presented to the house. The hon. member for Macleod pointed out that it was a reflection on the present librarians, and the minister agreed wholeheartedly with that interpretation.
I cannot see how it is any reflection whatever on the present librarians who have been commended from all sides of the house. As I mentioned the other day when this subject was up, it is no more a reflection on the present librarians than is the bill itself. Then the minister pointed out that the present librarians could not have been appointed if this amendment had been in the act at that time. Of course, that does not mean anything because there were no library schools and no degrees given at that time.

Library of Parliament Act
There was some complaint, too, that this amendment would be too restrictive and there would be a limited number of people from whom to choose for these positions because of the demand for these degrees. It seems to me that suggesting the qualifications as set down by the Canadian library association is the sensible way to do it, because the librarians themselves have set their own standards and surely they are the best judges. If there are schools not included in the Canadian library association's list, then all they have to do is raise their standards to meet the qualifications set down by that organization.
The hon. member for Timiskaming introduced another red herring. She said if we were to go into this degree business to such an extent the Minister of National Health and Welfare would be without a job, because he has not a medical degree. Then she asked what we would do in those circumstances. Well, that was a real red herring. I do not consider that a parallel situation at all. As I understand the situation the minister is the policymaker in his department, and the deputy minister is an administrator. It is a fact that the deputy minister of national health and welfare is a doctor. It is also true that the deputy minister of national defence is a soldier.
One hon. member said the chief librarian should have administrative ability, and that therefore the bill should be passed. Of course it is true that the chief librarian does have to have administrative ability. But the degree of bachelor of library science naturally includes administrative training and ability. So I would point out that my amendment is simply to safeguard against the library of parliament becoming a vehicle for political patronage. It is a recognition of the standards that librarians have sought for themselves as a profession.

But I am troubled by the amendment from another point of view. The hon. lady, in proposing the amendment, said this, as reported at page 4842 of Hansard:
I have been told by the Canadian library association that there are two library schools in Canada accredited by the American library association. These are the library schools of the universities of McGill and Toronto.

Moreover, if this is meant to imply that these are the only library schools accredited by the Canadian library association, that would exclude the graduates of any other Canadian library school. I am wondering whether that would not embarrass any administration that might be in office in carrying out the conventions of the constitution, that when the librarian is a person whose mother tongue is English the associate librarian shall be one whose mother tongue is French, or vice versa. I do think that is a very important point. The observance of that convention, particularly in the library which serves this chamber, is more important than any of the other qualifications; because if there is to be equal treatment for all members, regardless of which of the official languages happens to be their mother tongue, it is really essential that one of the two senior officers in the library of parliament should be able to talk freely in the language such members habitually use.

I have been trying to follow this debate ever since the bill was introduced. I recollect that when the matter was up for discussion in April 1954 it was gone into fairly fully. A certain situation arose in the library because of the damage caused by fire and water. At that time there was considerable difficulty in procuring the staff necessary to do the work of re-examining and reclassifying the books.
When the librarian made his report he said that with the staff he had available it would take him 20 years to complete the job he had on hand. If he had additional help he could possibly speed it up. In fact, he went so far as to say that to do the work he had to borrow personnel from the national library, from the University of Toronto and from McGill University. To do the necessary work required long hours. If my memory is correct, he said the work was done mostly by women. The hours were so long that it was beyond their physical capacity.
A review of the whole situation so far as it affected the library of the House of Commons was made. They said the system of cataloguing the books was out of date; that it was done now according to the library of congress techniques in the United States.

He said that suitable help was not procurable. I asked what salaries were being paid at that time. He said that a cataloguer received something in the neighbourhood of $3,800, and that they had difficulty in getting them. Questions were asked about the qualifications, whether they would require a degree in library science in future in order to occupy the position of librarian in the House of Commons and whether henceforth all applicants would be required to have that degree.
I did not take the trouble to ask just what universities or colleges gave degrees in library science, but I had the impression at that time that there were four in Canada. The librarian did not name them. 1 presume that at that time the staff came from the national library and from the universities of Toronto and McGill. He said there were four colleges who were recognized as giving degrees in library science, and there were quite a host of others in the Dominion of Canada who were not recognized but were training librarians. The latter were not recognized by the American library association.
He went on to discuss the matter of salaries that were paid; and when we were told that the salaries were so meagre or parsimonious as $3,800 for a qualified librarian, and particularly degree men, I said there were men in the departments who had no degrees at all who were getting much higher salaries. A committee was set up and a report was brought in.
I do not think there is any objection to the bill as it stands, except that it is not necessary for one in the position of librarian to have a degree in library science. The impression left in the minds of the members sitting on that committee was that in order to qualify for a position of any sort in the library a person would have to have this degree. It now turns out that this is not necessary; it turns out that not everyone must have this degree. It was brought out by the librarian in setting out the qualifications that he has competent people in his department.
Furthermore he said it was understaffed and could not possibly do what it had to do, particularly with the cramped quarters in which it must operate at the present time. But he does have within his employ a staff which is competent and capable of taking over. He did not say whether they had degrees, because this degree of library science has come into being only in the last 15 or 16 years. The librarian himself does not have this degree of bachelor of library science, but if he were asked to write one of these
Library of Parliament Act examinations I have not the slightest doubt that he would have the necessary qualifications.
Many people have come to the top through hard work; they have come up the hard way by learning as they went. He has imparted that knowledge to those who may succeed him. That is the best of all degrees. In my time I have had young men who have just come out of university turned over to me for further education in the chosen lines which they were to follow. I never had the benefit of university training, but they were turned over to me to round out their education.
I think the same thing applies as far as the librarian is concerned. We have a competent man in there and now they are trying to make the library staff into a semi-exclusive club. If people want to enter into the library they will say, "So far can you go and no farther". When a man gets near the top it may turn out that he cannot go any further because it has been set down here that he must possess certain attributes for the top job. It is said he must understand parliamentary procedure, constitutional authority; that he must have had training in finance and engineering and administration. He must have all these qualifications, with a knowledge of what the ministers and members may want, and sometimes anticipate it.
But if they do not pay a salary even equal to that of a high class bank manager, how can they require these qualifications for a head librarian? He would be just out of this world if he had all those qualifications. The rest of the staff are being told, "Oh, not for you this juicy plum. You are just too dumb." That is just about what it adds up to.
The only objection we have to this bill as it stands is that you are making the position unobtainable for those who are working in the library. You are telling them they must undergo the training and do the things that are necessary to be done, but when it comes to filling the position with a high salary, that is to be a different story.
All this has been very educational. I was glad I got the information on this matter. There were a lot of things I learned about what they had to do in order to supply information to members of this house. It certainly is a job that not everyone could aspire to. This job has been taken out of the hands of the civil service commission because people are not anxious to work in the library. They cannot secure applicants because there is no allure or incentive. There is no future in the job because of the salary being paid.

I understand in recent years an increase was granted, but the salaries are still not what they must be if you are going to insist on this qualification that they have this degree. It would also be better that the employing be turned back to the civil service commission in order that they may fill any vacancies. However, probably things will remain as they are. The hon. minister of fish stories the other day gave what might be termed a piscatorial narration. He implied that we were trying to make the library staff like a union.
The hon. member for Lanark referred to the medical and legal professions, which are governed by certain qualifications. I think it is only just and right if you are going to have a system for securing help in your library that you should be able to give the jobs to those qualifying. If the applicants have not the necessary training you should train them for the job; then when they get to the top they will be able to handle it without having to bring in any outsiders to look after it.

Does the government intend to appoint as general librarian a political itinerant whose qualifications do not include the possession of any university or library science degrees or the like, but which have been restricted to those of an assistant in a minister's office. The purpose of this' bill is to abolish the post of general librarian, so there will be no question about anyone being appointed to that position if the bill passes. Neither the position of general librarian nor parliamentary librarian will be abolished as long as the present incumbents continue in office. I know of no project to terminate the tenure of either incumbent. I am perfectly certain that the government has no one in mind for these appointments, and that there will be no one in mind until the time comes to make them.
I must say that my colleagues and I are flattered by the apparent assumption by hon. gentlemen immediately opposite that we will still be in office to make the appointments under this bill. I think they are justified in that assumption, but it rather surprised me because this restriction, until the act is amended again, would apply to any group of people who occupied the treasury benches.
I would be sorry to think that, if by some miracle hon. gentlemen opposite were translated to this side of the house, the hon. member for Danforth, for whom I have great esteem, could never hope to become parliamentary librarian.
I think the hon. member for Danforth was under a misapprehension about the bill, as it does not exclude any member of the library staff or anyone who is not a member of the library staff. It is the amendment that would do the excluding. The bill would leave it to the governor in council; and of course, because these appointments are made on the recommendation of the prime minister, that would leave to the prime minister of the day the recommendation as to the most suitable person to appoint.
As I pointed out when this bill was before the house previously, when appointments have been made by the party which now occupies the treasury benches, since confederation, they have invariably been made from the staff of the library; and when appointments have been made by the party of hon. gentlemen opposite, or the antecedents of the party-because they had different names in those days-of hon. gentlemen opposite, they have invariably been drawn from outside the staff of the library.
If we should occupy the treasury benches when either of these appointments came to be made, I think it is most unlikely that, with the competent staff that everybody in the committee has agreed the library has, it would be necessary to go outside the staff of the library to make an appointment. But I would not like to think that, if there were some eminent person available-say, for example, the head of another library-though he might

not have had a degree from McGill or Toronto, he would therefore be ineligible and the governor in council at that time could not appoint him. I would not like to think that even some eminent privy councillor like Hon. Martin Burrell who, if he happened to be available and who had great knowledge of constitutional law and parliamentary procedure and great learning, would be rendered technically ineligible because he did not happen to have a degree, or that some civil servant in the same position might not be transferred to this position if it seemed at the time that he was the best qualified person. The position of librarian is assimilated under our constitution to the position of a deputy minister, and in none of our statutes are any fetters put upon the choice of the governor in council in appointing a deputy minister.

It is quite wrong to say that the deputy minister of my hon. friend's department must be a doctor. There is no such regulation whatsoever in the statutes. I think there would be two views about whether a doctor is necessarily the most suitable person for the administrative head of a great department of state.
It is only a few days ago that hon. gentlemen opposite and newspapers supporting them were criticizing us because a distinguished airman who had undertaken to retire from the air force and become a civilian was being appointed as deputy minister of national defence. They were criticizing us because they said he would be too service-minded for this civilian post; and I agree that it is a civilian post and that it should be a civilian post.
As I said, I thought the hon. member for Greenwood shared with me the view that there was something to be said for the distinguished amateur. At any rate I am unrepentant in my view that while you obviously must have professional people for professional jobs, when you come to this kind of position requiring not only administrative skill but learning, I believe that general education and particularly a familiarity with constitutional history and constitutional law is apt to provide a better kind of qualification for a parliamentary librarian even than training in a library school; though if you could get both together, I think that would be still better.
I certainly do not for one moment want to suggest that I think people who went through library schools should be excluded. I do not think that. To any reasonable person I think that such training would commend 50433-336$
