But I should not like to see us obliged to take a second choice because he happened to have this degree, and drop as the first choice someone we thought to be a better man or a better woman because that man or woman did not happen to have taken this particular library course. That is the whole position the government has taken.

Of course I recall the time the present librarian was appointed, and I remember all the lobbying and so on that was indulged in in the house by some politicians who had an ambition to become librarians. Before I sit down may I say that I think the present staff of the library is competent and that it has been competent ever since I have been in the house. When Hon. Not only am I happy with the recommendation of the library committee, which I approve, that we shall have a librarian and an associate librarian; I also approve the suggestion that one of these shall be Englishspeaking and one shall be proficient in the other official language of our country; that is, French-speaking. I should like to see the House of Commons provided, perhaps in association with the library, with some competent research personnel who could give further assistance to members of parliament in their research. I say that, although it does not come within the orbit of this particular bill. While I realize there is some logic in what the minister has said, nevertheless, believing as I do that some limitation should be placed upon the government with regard to an important appointment of this kind, I am going to support the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE

Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to bring to your attention a matter of keen concern, I believe, to this house, the other chamber and people generally throughout the country. I refer to the long discussed question of reform of the Senate.
Oh, oh.

I am not surprised, Mr. Speaker, that those to your right should laugh, because this important issue has become almost a national joke. However, there never was a time in our history when we should laugh less at our parliamentary institutions, so well established and designed for the government of this country, than at this time when many other countries of the world have lost their democratic freedom. I believe we might justly be prouder of our institutions today than at any other time in our history. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there never was a time when hon. members of this house, no matter from what district they come, were more challenged to preserve carefully the basic and fundamental principles of our parliamentary institutions.
One of the most important of these institutions is the other house, the Senate of Canada. Long before we had a British North America Act the upper house was recognized. There are few countries in the world where the upper chamber has not been recognized, although perhaps in different forms than that which is laid down for us.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, it was one of the fathers of confederation, Sir John A. Macdonald, who found it would be possible to bring the provinces together by guaranteeing minority rights and the rights of the provinces by the establishment of the Senate of Canada. That is borne out by the statements made at that time, which indicate that it was not to be a forum that would become so strong as to be in conflict with the Commons. They believed the role of the Senate would be that of a restraining influence. It would be a body that could revise hasty legislation that might be passed in this house. It would not be responsible to popular sentiment or appeal throughout the country, but as a result of Senate action people generally would have time to use their collective common sense and assert themselves.
5330	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform
It was also suggested that in the minds of the fathers of confederation the members of the Senate were to act more or less in the role of judges of what we do in this house. They were not to be partisan supporters or blind admirers of everything the government might do. Its members were to be selected from amongst men who would lend dignity and distinction to the public life of Canada. They were to be chosen for their acknowledged achievements or for their moral and intellectual qualities, and were to be placed in a position high above the tide of party strife. It was thought that senators so appointed would invest their decisions with a moral authority in the country which no popular leader could afford to wholly disregard. In other words they were to become more or less the safety valve of this house.
In order to better ensure the impartiality and independence of their decisions, like those appointed to the bench, senators were not to be appointed for a term of years but for life. Such a senate would, in the first place, exercise an immense influence upon public opinion. Being men of experienced judgment they would know that in any conflict they must give way to the elected representatives of the people. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that it was carefully designed not to conflict with the authority of parliament, but was to be composed of men who were impartial, to act more or less in the role of judges in order that this house might take cognizance of their leadership in many respects. At no time was it intended that they should be in conflict with or take away from the authority of this house. As I have said, they were to act more or less as a safety valve.
If those men were living today how gravely disappointed they would be; because I feel that the result has been more or less the opposite. I am not going to go into details. It does appear to me that there has been a different attitude towards that constituted body as set out in the British North America Act. Down through the years there has been a different attitude as between those who sit to your right and form the government today and those of us who represent the other old historic party that is now Her Majesty's loyal opposition. Back in 1893 the Liberal party clamoured in its convention for a reform or abolishment of the Senate. The Liberal party was in power for 15 years, and they had a substantial majority in the Senate. The Senate defeated important measures of Sir Robert Borden's government, one of which was the building of three dreadnoughts for the British navy.


Our party sitting here today is not asking for the abolition of the Senate. I am not expressing sentiments that only emanate from this side of the house. The Senate has been the laughing stock of public administration for almost half a century. Only recently a member of the upper house moved a motion requesting the filling of some 21 or 22 existing vacancies. Today there are vacancies in the Senate representation from every province but two, and now 22 districts are not represented at all.
However, that is not the issue. I am not following exactly what the elder statesman in the other place moved the other day. He asked whether or not the Senate was dying. On another occasion he wondered if it were dead. In fact I think every senator is now wondering when it will die a natural death, as it will if these positions are not filled. Some time ago the Prime Minister said there were going to be new appointments, and as an almost modest political gesture he did suggest appointing those who were not blind admirers of his government. We have not heard very much of that suggestion since, because I noticed there were a lot of hungry people in his own party who did not seem to like that suggestion.
We are not arguing for the abolition of the Senate. As the leading senator mentioned in his motion, he is fearful of it being abolished instead of being reformed. We are quite aware of the fact that there are different things that could be done in order to reform it. We must have an amendment to the British North America Act, and unlike the House of Lords in the United Kingdom such an amendment must be approved by the house and by the Senate. The government could proceed to sound out the feeling of the Senate and try to amend the British North America Act to reform the Senate, as they long since promised. They could, on the other hand, proceed as they are doing and neglect to fill the vacancies. When one looks over the ages of the senators one sees that it is possible for the lord of the Liberal party to abolish the Senate by natural procedure.
But that is not the policy of the party as announced by those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, for at least the last 30 years. I can well recall that when I first entered the House of Commons, the late Mr. Mackenzie King campaigned in my riding. His former secretary laughs, and he should laugh at it. If the late right hon. gentleman were alive today he would laugh at it himself. He campaigned in North York and other places, and said he was going to reform the Senate. He

had wanted to reform it for some time, and he was going to reform it. How did he reform it? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) knows how he reformed it. It was the talk of the barber shops, garages, and other places in his constituency as well as mine. He reformed it by appointing more reformers to the Senate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The very best way.

Exactly. I shall proceed to show by his own words that it was the only way to do it. This was the attitude of the party that played with this like a cat would play with a mouse or like less amateur politicians would kick it around as a political football, so it would affect our whole constitutional form of government.
There was a difference in attitude as was set out by the different leaders. Different statements were made by former leaders of the party I have the honour to represent today and the leaders of whom the Minister of Finance nods approval. I might point out that in a debate in 1865 Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald pointed out that while he would like to have an image of the House of Lords in Great Britain, as then constituted, in order to appease certain elements across the country he would see that there were four different districts, with 24 senators from the maritimes, 24 from western Canada, 24 from Quebec and 24 from Ontario. Now there are 6 from Newfoundland, with the government still holding the power to put more reformers in by holding 8 more that they can name, if they wish.
I hesitate to read all that was said. However, I would point out that Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald said that it was most important to have a senate or an upper house, as did Sir Wilfrid Laurier on occasions. Sir John A. Macdonald said:
In order to protect local interests, and to prevent sectional jealousies, it was found requisite that the three great divisions into which British North America is separated, should be represented in the Upper House on the principle of equality. There are three great sections, having different interests, in this proposed confederation. We have western Canada, an agricultural country far away from the sea, and having the largest population who have agricultural interests principally to guard. We have lower Canada, with other and separate interests, and especially with institutions and laws which she jealously guards against absorption by any larger, more numerous or stronger power. And we have the maritime provinces, having also different sectional interests of their own, having, from their position, classes and interest which we do not know in western Canada. Accordingly, in the Upper House-the controlling and regulating, but not the initiating branch (for we know that here as in England, to the lower house will practically belong the initiation of matters of great public interest), in the house which has the
Proposed Senate Reform sober second thought in legislation-it is provided that each of those great sections shall be represented equally by 24 members.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a matter of certain proposals that have been made. It is not a matter today of whether we are going to have a ten-year term for senators. Nor is it a matter of whether we say they should retire at the age of 75 years. I am not sure that the Prime Minister even would agree with that. It is not a matter as to whether they should be elected by ballot. It is not a matter whether, as has been suggested, some should be elected and some appointed by the government. It is not a matter of whether they should be nominated by the provinces, as someone has suggested.
Mr. Speaker, over the last quarter century there have been many similar proposals. We hear people saying that the Senate should be more representative than it is today. We certainly do not believe there should be 22 vacancies in it. That certainly never was the intention under the British North America Act. Even the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
A second chamber is an absolutely needed safeguard for the smaller provinces against a possible invasion of their rights by the larger provinces.
There was very little criticism of or opposition to the early set-up. But you could see the beginning of the difference in attitude between those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, and those of us who sit to your left and represent the other old historic party. First we have what was said by Sir Oliver Mowat prior to the Liberal convention in 1893. These were his words:
The present constitution of the Senate is inconsistent with the federal principle in our system of government, and is in other respects defective, as it makes the Senate independent of the people and uncontrolled by the public opinion of the country, and should be so amended as to bring it into harmony with the principles of popular government.
You will observe a distinct difference between that and the intention of the fathers of confederation, who intended just the opposite, I suggest. And at the Liberal party convention in Ottawa in 1893 it was moved:
We are agreed as to the necessity of a fundamental reformation of the Senate-if for any reason a Senate must be or should be retained. The Senate as now constituted is the weakest point in our constitution.
Another prominent Liberal of those days, Sir Richard Cartwright, also indicated that to have the Senate constituted as was intended originally, along non-political lines, was not satisfactory even to the party in that day. He said:
I think, sir, we all agree that the constitution of the Senate, as it at present exists, is a blot upon popular government and free institutions.

Proposed Senate Reform
I shall not go further, except to show how consistent the Liberal party has been along these lines in the last number of years. I say that as to responsibility for the disintegration, ineffectiveness and lack of popular appeal by the Senate in this country, most certainly no body is more to blame than the Liberal party that has been in office for the last 25 years, and has been making a joke of Senate reform.
Twenty years.

Since long before the hon. member was here, back in those days when he was taking more interest in other things and did not notice what was going on in the party to which he belongs.
I could cite many instances. I have said in this House of Commons on different occasions what should be done. The late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, and his party, were committed to the reform of the Senate. But now we find, as I say, that it is becoming a joke in administrative circles in Canada.
I know it was suggested from different parts of the house years ago that we should have an elected senate. It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who pointed out that it should be strengthened. Those who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, have said that to have an elected senate would create two different houses and lead to confusion. Others have said that the Senate should be partly elected and partly appointed. But most certainly no one has suggested at any time from this side of the house that the Senate of Canada should simply swallow what is done in the House of Commons, that it should be absolutely in line with the popular party of the day and in support of the government.
I can well recall how back some years ago the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, who was then prime minister, was disgusted with the Senate because on two or three occasions they had opposed certain legislation that had passed the House of Commons. That legislation was not readily approved in the other house. Hansard for 1924 will show where Mr. Mackenzie King said:
Hon. members will recall that at the close of last session, and at the close of the preceding session, bills which were passed by this house and which touched matters that are very vital to the electorate failed of enactment owing to the action of the Senate.
Then he continued:
This year we have instances of bills that have passed this house in three separate sessions of parliament, and which have been rejected each time by the second chamber.
Mr. Speaker, there never was a time in our history that this house needed a check more than it has in the last few years, when there


has been a clamouring to do those things that were popular, no matter what they were. There never was a time in our history when that was more needed. Our wise old forefathers must have foreseen that there would be those who would give anyone anything, for their votes. The late Mr. King and his party stated on different occasions as far back as the 1925 election, in which I took some part myself, what their position was with respect to the Senate. In one of his speeches he said:
Only a few days ago a number of senators were appointed. Every one has given me his pledged word he will be prepared, once a measure passes the commons, to give it his support. Subsequent senators will be appointed with that understanding, and as Providence takes away a few of the older members, you will have a Senate pledged to bring about the reforms for which the administration stands.
In other words these men were pledged. He made the statement on different occasions that the only way the Senate could be reformed would be from within. He was fully convinced of the necessity of bringing it to the attention of parliament. He said there were two great obstacles to this objective. One was the obstruction of the Senate and its influence on the party. He made the statement from many a platform that his party would bring reform into effect immediately.
The late Mr. King was in office following 1925, and surely there is not a member within sound of my voice who has any recollection of politics during those years who does not realize that one of the most important issues in that campaign-in fact for several years previously the late Mr. King had suggested that he would bring it up at an election time, except he did not think the people were ripe for it-was Senate reform. I heard him say in this house how important it was that it be brought up, and it was made an election issue.
I quote from the Globe and Mail of those days as further evidence of what I heard from various platforms. He went on to point out that we must have a Senate that had some respect for the popular opinion of the country, and he said:
Even more arbitrary has been the Senate's action in rejecting measures which have passed the House of Commons and been sent to the Senate a second and third time. If the Senate is to be made more responsive to the popular will, then the popular will with respect to the Senate must make itself known and felt.
Further he said:
To amend the constitution and the powers of the Senate, two steps are necessary. The Senate itself must be a party to the reform recommended, and the imperial parliament must act. Before the imperial parliament would enact the necessary

legislation by way of amendment to the British North America Act, it would expect on a matter of this kind an address of both houses of the Canadian parliament. It is reasonable to assume, that upon such an address from both houses it would not hesitate to act. There are two ways of bringing about accord between the two houses in the matter of an address to the imperial parliament: One, the indirect method of summoning a conference of representatives of all the provinces of the dominion and seeking at such a gathering to obtain unanimity of view with respect to the amendments of the constitution and powers of the Senate. The other, the appointment of senators prepared to accept Senate reform. An agreement reached at such a conference if introduced in the form of a resolution would scarcely fail to pass both houses.
He went on to point out that the only way it could be reformed would be from within, in these words:
Reform from within can be effected only by making certain of the presence in the Senate of a sufficient number of members who can be relied upon to support and carry through that chamber whatever measure of Senate reform may be sent from the commons as a part of government policy. In this great and good work Providence has been aiding the Liberal party. When we came into office the Tory majority was 26. At the close of the last session of parliament it was 22. Yesterday it was 23. Today, I am happy to say, it has been reduced to 15 through the appointment within the past 24 hours of eight senators, each of whom has expressed his intention of supporting whatever measure of Senate reform the present government may submit in furtherance of its policy to bring the constitution and powers of that body more into accord with the spirit of the times in which we live. In the course of a few days it will be reduced to 13 by the filling of two remaining vacancies. That is an unlucky number for the Tory majority that remains.
And so it was.
In Great Britain the method employed to secure the enactment in the House of Lords of measures which have passed the commons and been rejected by the Lords has been to create or threaten the creation of extra peers, pledged to give the commons the necessary support.
In as much as the government controls appointments to the Senate, on a question like reform of the Senate the government is more or less in a position to secure support for its measures once the number of its appointees is sufficient to give it a majority in that house. That is the only certain way. I think I can say of the senators who have been appointed by a Liberal administration, whether of Sir Wilfrid's administration or the present administration, that all are sufficiently Liberal to give their support to any reasonable measure of Senate reform which the present government may propose. I know I can say of those who have just been appointed that one and all have expressed their willingness to champion the cause of Senate reform, and I shall undertake to say that no further appointments will be made by the present government to the Senate except upon the distinct understanding that the appointee will give wholehearted advocacy and support to any measure of Senate reform the government, as a part of government policy, may ask both houses of parliament to adopt.
So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to know about these senators and whether they have
Proposed Senate Reform violated their trust. Have these elder statesmen in the other place made a solemn pledge to the Liberal party that they will do what they were asked to do so far as Senate reform is concerned? Have they all made solemn pledges? Some of them have indicated they have not. Some have made motions to have vacancies filled, but none has made a move to reform the Senate as it stands.
The late Prime Minister King was so adamant in this that he made it part of the policy of his party. Once they had a majority that was what they were supposed to do; but they have had a top-heavy, lopsided majority for some time and the reputation of the Senate has fallen because it has been played with for political purposes. The Senate was to be reformed. In every Liberal campaign we have had in the last quarter of a century it was said that some change was to be made in the Senate. It was always hinted how it was to be reformed.
The last hint given by the present Prime Minister was the most attractive of all. He was generous. He was going to name-I do not know that he said he was going to name any Tories-every stripe that would not conflict with his highly motivated policy. The late prime minister said he was anxious to see responsible government upheld to the utmost. He was the champion of responsible government. He should be here now. The late prime minister said:
But just because I am anxious that responsible government shall be upheld to the utmost, I have been careful to make sure of the ground before taking a decisive step. Had I gone to the country on this issue a year ago, as I am told I should have done, I am not convinced that its importance would have been appreciated as fully as it is today.
Again he said:
Of this at least I have certain knowledge, I would not have had the eight good men and true who were appointed yesterday, and who are pledged to Senate reform and the two more to be appointed and who will join their efforts to other appointees of the Liberal party in bringing about this all-important feature of Liberal policy. May I say that the government has decided without further delay to meet the issue of responsible government raised by the Senate, and I now ask the Liberal press of this country, as well as all who desire to see Liberal traditions and principles upheld, to join me in making Senate reform a certainty in the only way that is at all likely to accomplish that end.
As has been truly said, "A vote for a Liberal candidate is a vote to bring the Senate into line with the Liberal government and the House of
Commons."
Just imagine the difference between that statement and the statements made by some of the other statesmen. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this is outstanding and glittering evidence of the difference between the party
5334	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform that sits to your right and the policy of this other old historic party, Her Majesty's loyal opposition. Mr. King said:
"A vote for a Liberal candidate is a vote to bring the Senate into line with the Liberal government and the House of Commons."
When the late Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald was inaugurating this policy he tried to make the Senate the safety valve for parliamentary institutions that it has been, Mr. Speaker, despite the last few years. It shall be again a great safety valve for our democratic way of life. I am proud of our parliamentary institutions, as we all are. We have more reason to be proud of them today than ever before because of what we see happening all over the world. Sir John A. Macdonald said:
There would be no use of an upper house if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing or amending or postponing the legislation of the lower house. It would be of no value whatever were it a mere chamber for registering the decrees of the lower house. It must be an independent house having a free action of its own, for it is only valuable as being a regulating body, calmly considering the legislation initiated by the popular branch, and preventing any hasty or ill-considered legislation which may come from that body, but it will never set itself in opposition against the deliberate and understood wishes of the people.
Mr. Speaker, I hope you have observed the clean-cut distinction between those two statements. The late Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald was not the only man who saw the benefit of the original purposes of this important part of our parliamentary institution. The late Right Hon. Sir Clifford Sifton, who could not be said to always have been in agreement with the late Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald, or vice versa, said when debating this issue:
No nation should be under unchecked, singlechamber government. The democracy must rule, but it is expedient that, in critical cases, it should have an opportunity to think twice. According to my experience, the will of the people is very often better expressed after a check, and after a period of searching and critical discussion which generally arises from such a check, than it is in the first instance.
Then in 1926 and 1927 the prime minister of that day was asked several questions by Mr. Evans, then a member of the house. He was asked:
1.	What is the form or wording of the pledge, if any, taken from those who have been appointed senators during the last two years with a view to Senate reform?
2.	How many have thus been pledged?
The prime minister replied:
An assurance of support of such measure of Senate reform, in conformity with the requirements of the constitution, as may be introduced by the Liberal administration.
This assurance has been given by all who have accepted appointment to the Senate within the time mentioned.


That is from page 355 of Hansard for 192627. Then the prime minister was asked this question by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, as reported on page 2332 of Hansard of 1940:
I would ask the Prime Minister, in view of the difficulty that has arisen, whether he will consider his long-promised reform of the Senate at the next session of parliament?
The answer was:
That is something X have been considering all my life.
When you think of all the things he did throughout his life; when you realize that the same tactics were used in connection with the reform of the Senate as in connection with party policy and fiscal and other matters, we realize that had it not been for radio and television they would have been able to go ahead and talk free trade in one part of the country and protection in the other, reform of the Senate in one part of the country and the protection of provincial rights in another.
I believe it is a matter of national concern that the Senate be not abolished. I believe that everyone who is familiar with the progressive history of our parliamentary institutions will agree that the Senate should be restored to the position it was intended to fill. We do not want it abolished; we do not want it disintegrated; we are not asking that certain appointments be made, but the fact is that they have not been as they were intended to be.
For over 30 years the party to your right have promised Senate reform. They have set out the reasons why they could not carry it out. Those reasons have disappeared, yet they still hesitate to move. Therefore we are not apologizing; I am not apologizing for the party for bringing this matter before the house at this late date in the session.
This matter has been kicked around for many years. Those who have read the history of this country know very well that no matter how strong any party might be in this country, it was never intended by those who designed the constitution of this country better than they knew that the Senate should develop into a rubber stamp for the Liberal party. It never was intended to be that. It never was intended that it should be disregarded as it has been, with about one-quarter of the seats not filled. It never was intended to be an institution to be filled with ward heelers, those who had supported the party financially and morally. It never was intended that the chief qualification for the Senate should be blind allegiance to any government. Our pioneer forefather statesmen intended the Senate to be a body of

men who were independent like those on our benches, to be more like judges than partisans. The fact is that it has turned out to be almost the opposite.
I realize that it is always a little difficult to discuss the actions of the other house. We have keen respect for our institutions, and we have keen respect for the incumbents. Many of them are men who have been successful in different walks of life. Many of them have been successful in parliamentary service. Some of them were hardly heard of before they came to the Senate, and others have hardly been heard since they came to the Senate. However, they were the choice of the government in those days; but I do submit that it was meant that their qualifications should be more than merely having been supporters of the government.
I have tried to emphasize that the party to which I belong has urged down through the years, not only in the days of the late Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald, the late Sir Robert Borden and the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen and others, that more use should be made of the Senate.
I realize, as I said at the outset, that there has been no time in the history of this dominion when a safety valve such as the Senate was more important. There is not an experienced politician within sound of my voice who does not know that with all parties trying to achieve power, with a party with a top-heavy majority trying to stay in power, almost any suggestion by a municipal council, a mayor or reeve across Canada is being taken up, and if one cabinet minister is a little more conservative in these matters, then another cabinet minister will reach in and say, "That should be suggested." They will do anything for temporary popularity.
Therefore we need this safety valve so there will be time for reflection, so the all-powerful and all-intelligent public, individually and collectively, may have time to reflect. We need the Senate. It should not be made innocuous, but it has been neutralized by the actions of this government. It is being laughed at by the public. It has proved ineffective in administration, and the responsibility lies exactly on the doorstep of those who sit to your right, those who have promised and heralded Senate reform at election time but who excused themselves by saying they had not the power. Those excuses cannot be made at this time.
Therefore I feel it is highly proper that we should have our institutions as they were established, and that they should be carried out in the way intended. We have urged this upon the government. The government have 50433-337}
Proposed Senate Reform even ignored their own proposals. Therefore we ask them to acknowledge and recognize ours. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"the government should give consideration to initiating the necessary consultation and inquiry respecting reform of the Senate so that all appropriate steps may be taken, including such matters as the method by which the members of the Senate should be chosen and their tenure of office so that the Senate may more effectively discharge the constitutional function it was intended to serve as an integral part of our parliamentary system."

Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): Mr. Speaker, because the position of this party and this movement with respect to the Senate is so well known, my remarks on this occasion will be brief.
While the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has been speaking, I have been looking with some interest over a debate which took place on May 31, 1954. It was very similar to the one that seems to be in progress at the present time. I must assure Your Honour that what happens now will not parallel exactly what happened last time. In other words, we shall not try to move again the subamendment which Your Honour ruled out of order last year. However, perhaps I might be permitted to read the amendment which was moved on that occasion by my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), which was as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the word "respecting" and by substituting therefor the following words: "the steps to be taken to secure the abolition of the Senate".
In terms of fitting it into the amendment which is now before the house, that subamendment of May 31, 1954, would be as appropriate today as it was then. However, as reported at page 5259 of Hansard of last year, Your Honour suggested, after some discussion, that abolition was not exactly a
5336	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform method of reform. Your Honour thought that was rather drastic reform and that it should be the subject of another motion rather than of a subamendment. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, since to move this subamendment again would only result in Your Honour being consistent and giving the same ruling, we shall not move the subamendment, although by having read it I have indicated the position that we of the C.C.F. take with regard to the Senate, which is that it should be abolished.
I have been wondering too, Mr. Speaker, whether the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) might be stealing that plank from the C.C.F. platform. He has not yet announced that he agrees with us that the Senate should be abolished, but he seems to be abolishing it just by allowing its membership to decrease. This failure to fill the vacancies, to which we take no exception, if continued for a period of time could result in the abolition of the Senate. It may be that once again the party on the other side of the house is stealing a plank from the C.C.F. platform.
Many of the things I might have said in support of our contention that the Senate should be abolished have, in fact, been said today by the acting leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). The critical remarks and comments he has made as to the position the Senate occupies in public opinion today are, we suggest, all reasons why the Senate might well be abolished.
We feel that Canadian democracy has grown up. We feel that the situation today is unlike the situation back in 1867, when our forefathers felt there should be some check on the elected representatives. We feel that the day has come when our parliament should be an entirely responsible body. When we say "responsible" we mean that it should be responsible to the people. We do not see how you can carry that idea of responsibility through to its logical conclusion when you have, with power equal to that of the elected house, a body which is not elected by the people at all.
The suggested reform which comes from some quarters to the effect that the Senate might be elected would just make for duplication, I suggest. On the other hand, if you found ways of strengthening it by changing the method of appointment or in other ways, you would simply continue as part of our parliamentary institution a body that is not responsible to the people of this country. We feel that in the final analysis this is not in keeping with the principles of democracy. That is the reason our C.C.F. movement


across the years has felt that the kind of reform most appropriate for the Senate would be its abolition.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I am going to suggest that if hon. members to the right want a reform, here is one specific reform they might advocate. I have here a copy of the Senate Hansard for last session. I refer to the session of 1953-54. Hon. members will note that it consists of one bound volume. I have as well a ruler in my hand, and I find that the thickness of this volume is 1J inches.
They don't have Stanley Knowles.

of them. That makes 367 members of parliament. If you multiply the height of this pile of material, which is 16 inches, by 367 it comes to a pile 489 feet high. As I have already indicated, we do not feel it is necessary to take a great deal of time on this question at this stage of our proceedings. As a matter of fact, when the issue was introduced by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe I procured my own file on Senate reform and Senate abolition and pulled out quite a number of quotations that have been placed on the record across the years. I am not going to offend against the rule respecting repetition, because the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has, one by one, given just about all the quotations I have in my file.
However, his point is well taken, namely that back in the early twenties the Liberal party made a major point of Senate reform. Mr. King was determined that the other house would be reformed, but as time went on it became more and more difficult for members of the opposition to get Mr. King to indicate when this reform was going to take place. In the meantime we feel, as I have already indicated, that democracy has grown up and that the time has come to have a fully responsible government and a fully responsible parliament in this country. Therefore, since we are in the position, in view of what happened last year, that we cannot move a subamendment stating the type of reform in which we believe, which is abolition, we shall support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe to indicate our dissatisfaction with the institution of the Senate as it now stands and our feeling that something very drastic should be done about it.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I recognize the hon. member for Macleod.

Mr. Speaker, I was not in the chamber when the amendment was introduced. I had other duties to perform. But since coming into the chamber I have read the amendment and I am convinced that we would be in favour of it
Proposed. Senate Reform. although, not having heard the speech introductory to the amendment, I do not know whether I would be in favour of the speech.
The amendment is subject to more than one interpretation. In general it calls for an inquiry into Senate reform. In the past this group has taken the position of being in favour of some Senate reform. Personally I have never quite brought myself to believe that the Senate should be abolished, because in my opinion it can perform a very useful function.
If my understanding of its function is correct I would suggest that from the constitutional point of view senators, appointed as they are by the governor in council, represent in a sense Her Majesty, and one of their prime functions constitutionally is to guard the rights of sovereign bodies. One of their functions is to protect and guard the rights of the legislatures of the provinces. To me that is a very important function, perhaps the most important constitutional function of the Senate, and I am convinced that the making of appointments in the way it has been done in the past, which has very often been described as appointments of good party supporters, is inclined to place lesser emphasis upon the prime function of the Senate and greater emphasis on protection by them of the government and the legislation the government introduces.
I am not going to say at the moment what type of reform might be beneficial. A number of suggestions have been made. It has been suggested before that members of the Senate should be elected by the people, as is done in the United States. That may be a very admirable procedure. Another suggestion is that the provinces, which are sovereign in their own right, should appoint a certain number of senators. Perhaps there could be a combination of the two, so many elected and so many appointed, or there could be a combination of two other methods. Perhaps the federal government could appoint some and the provinces could appoint some. All these suggestions could be made.
I appreciate that part of the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which I heard having to do with the actual work of the Senate. If an inquiry were instituted, that is a matter that could be investigated. How can they become more effective?
There is another very important point that strikes me. What is the attitude of the people of Canada toward the upper house? At the present time I am inclined to believe that the people of Canada are beginning to depreciate the value of our Senate to some extent. If there is one thing that is needed in any

Proposed Senate Reform parliamentary institution it is the confidence of the people, and if their confidence is depreciating to any extent then the matter should be looked into.
I know it is the consensus among a large proportion of the people of Canada that the Senate is of little value. I believe it can be made of some value. If it is not going to be made of some value, then of course the attitude that the Senate should be abolished will grow.
We may as well meet that situation, because it will have to be met sooner or later. As my colleague the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has whispered in my ear, if it is a dying party let us give it a decent burial, but if it is a body that should be made useful let us revive it and make it a healthy and functioning body in which the people of Canada will have confidence and of which they will be proud. That to me is a very important thing.
I notice the amendment reads in part as follows:
The government should give consideration to initiating the necessary consultation and inquiry respecting reform of the Senate . . .
What is intended by that I do not know. It is broad enough to involve an inquiry by the government. It is broad enough to involve even a joint parliamentary committee or it is broad enough to bring into existence a royal commission. I do not know that I am particularly in favour of that, but it is broad enough in scope to bring before the government the necessity of making some very extensive inquiry into the reform of the Senate in order that the Senate may be strong, and a body in which the Canadian people could have a good deal of confidence. Because of that, this group will support the amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
My first reaction to this particular motion is that perhaps it has been introduced a little late in the session. Nevertheless I feel that members of all parties will agree that there is merit in the Conservative suggestion. Certainly throughout Canada there is a distinct feeling that Senate reform is needed. I suppose that for almost 80 years Senate reform has been talked about in this house. Yet, so far as I know, there has not been one single major Senate reform measure introduced since confederation. The Senate today is pretty well the same as it was back in 1867.
At this moment, as other members have mentioned, it looks like the Senate is dying out of sheer neglect. I believe one hon. member pointed out that there are now 22 vacancies. Those vacancies exist despite the fact
[Mr. Hansell.l

it is the constitutional right of every province to have its proper share of members in the Senate. Many people throughout Canada are beginning to wonder if it is the deliberate intention of the government to let the Senate die.
I am not going to take the time of the house to go into the weaknesses of the Senate. They can be summed up very briefly. Members are appointed rather than elected; appointments appear to have been made as a reward for past political services instead of any particular ability. There are some parties in Canada, such as the C.C.F., Social Credit, Union Na-tionale, who have no representation at all in the Senate. Then there is the fact that there is no age limit. People who would be very useful in the Senate are kept out, and others who have outlived their usefulness are kept in the red chamber.
Moreover, hon. members will recall that some provinces are not fairly represented according to population. For instance, citizens in my province always find it strange that Saskatchewan should only have six senators with a population of almost 900,000, while New Brunswick with a population of slightly over 500,000 has ten senators.
Originally, if I remember my history, the Senate was set up for two main reasons. In the first place it was to be the chamber of second thought and sober consideration. In the second place it was believed to be a safeguard for the provinces, a safeguard for minority rights and particularly, I think perhaps, of the French-Canadian minority.
I believe history has proved that this safeguard is not needed. The French-Canadian population in Canada have their interests safeguarded (a) by the constitution; (b) by the courts; (c) by their federal members here in parliament; (d) by their cabinet ministers; (e) by the very way their population is growing. I do not believe any government, no matter of what party, would dare ignore the rights of the French-speaking minority today. I feel, therefore, that the original need of the Senate probably is no longer valid. For that reason I should like to see the Senate abolished. But if it is going to be continued I think we should be realistic. I think we should inaugurate reforms which will make the Senate an effective instrument and one which will have the respect of the Canadian people.
Now, what reforms should be adopted? Every member has his own ideas. Certainly there should be, as I mentioned a moment ago, an age limit. I like a scheme which would allow the provinces to appoint perhaps one-third of the members. I should like to see those members appointed for only four or

five years. This would ensure that all shades of political opinion in Canada would be represented. It would ensure, in the second place, that these short-term senators would do their work diligently so they might be reappointed.
Then the government should take steps to ensure that there is an opposition in the Senate. I should like to see members of other political parties appointed when the Prime Minister fills these 22 vacancies.
At the moment there is no representative of the trade unions in the Senate. I would suggest that Mr. Percy Bengough might be an ideal appointment for the Prime Minister to make when the time comes. I should like perhaps to see Mr. Graham Towers, the former head of the Bank of Canada, put in the Senate. I believe he would be a very useful member. I should like to see Mr. John Bracken, the former leader of the Conservatives, in the Senate. I think he could make a valuable contribution. I say again - that I believe the Senate should be abolished. But if it is not abolished, then let us reform it in such a way that it can be of practical use to the Canadian people.
I support this motion which has been moved by the Conservative group today. I know that not much can be done at this session. However, I hope that at the next session the house leader or the Prime Minister will give serious consideration to setting up a joint committee of both houses to go into this whole problem of Senate reform.

I am somewhat surprised, Mr. Speaker, that as yet no member of the government party has indicated any intention of taking part in this debate. I believe it is of such importance that the Prime Minister himself should tell the house and the country what are his views with regard to this problem of the Canadian Senate. I would point out to hon. members that this resolution urges that the government give consideration to initiating the necessary consultations and inquiries respecting reform of the Senate. Such action can only come from the government. If anything is to be done at all it will have to be initiated by those who sit to your right.
And at this session.

It should have been done long igo. I would point out also that the amendment refers to consultations and inquiries. I believe it would be wise to have a consultation on this problem with the various provinces before a solution is reached. Certainly some action of that kind will be required.
This resolution cites various subjects into which inquiry should be made. For example, mention was made in the original motion of
Proposed Senate Reform the tenure of office and the method of choosing appointees. These two subjects are not, of course, exclusive. There are several other principles having to do with Senate reform which should be included for consideration.
Furthermore, the resolution points out very clearly the objective of these consultations and inquiries, namely so the Senate may discharge its constitutional functions. 1 believe there is agreement in this chamber on the main functions of the Senate, namely that it should be a reviewing body, able to carry on in much the same way as a high court; to review legislation in a judicial frame of mind; and secondly, to protect minorities. It is perfectly obvious that was one of the main reasons for having a senate in Canada. It was felt that protection should be given to the maritimes when they came into confederation, and also to the province of Quebec. This was one of the original purposes of the fathers of confederation in providing for a senate. So much for the resolution, Mr. Speaker.
I go on to state that I believe there is need for action quickly if the Senate is to be preserved at all. If this question is allowed to drift indefinitely as it has in recent years, and if public opinion against the Senate increases steadily-certainly that is the case in British Columbia, and I have no doubt it is true in most of the other provinces-then surely something should be done about it. The Senate has never been lowpr in public esteem than it is at the present time.
The very mention of the Senate from a public platform brings smiles. We had that identical reaction here today when the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe indicated that he proposed to speak about Senate reform. When he said that, members in all parts of the chamber laughed, and I am afraid that merely reflected the thinking of Canadians from coast to coast. Let us not fool ourselves; the Senate no longer commands serious attention in the country. The fact is that it has been allowed to fall into decay.
That brings us to the question of where we should place the blame for the present low position of the Senate. I do not believe I can be contradicted successfully when I say that the blame for that condition rests squarely on two Liberal prime ministers of Canada, the first of whom was Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, and the second the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). Appointments to the Senate are in their discretion. They and they alone are responsible for the appointments made since 1921, with the exception of that period between 1930 and 1935, at which time Right Hon. Mr. Bennett was prime minister of Canada.

What was the attitude of Mr. King toward the Senate? I believe it can be accurately described as more or less hypocritical. When he first became prime minister he was faced with a hostile Senate. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has read from newspaper reports and from statements by Mr. King which indicate that he was annoyed about the fact that certain of his legislation was overruled by the Senate in which, at that time, the Liberal party did not have a majority. Mr. King used Senate reform as a plank with which to win elections both, I presume, in 1925 and again in 1926.
The hon. member has read statements which verify what we all know to be the truth, that in making appointments to the Senate Mr. King extracted a pledge from the appointees that they would do what he wished them to do with regard to reform of the Senate. The trouble, of course, was that once he got a majority in the Senate he no longer wanted to reform it. Therefore his pledgees or appointees, or whatever you wish to call them, were not called upon to put through any Liberal policy of Senate reform, because there was no such policy.
I thought the answer by Mr. King to questions asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in 1948 was very significant. That answer is found at page 853 of Hansard for that year. Mr. King did not choose to answer those questions in writing. He made a verbal reply and said in part:
His question relates to so-called pledges or undertakings given by certain members of the Liberal party at the time of their appointment to the Senate that they would, if the question of Senate reform came up, support in the Senate such legislation in that particular as the government of the day might wish to have enacted.
Then he went on to explain the reason he had obtained these pledges, and said:
It was that kind of thing which was in my mind when I spoke with different gentlemen before they were formally appointed to the Senate and received their assurance that, in situations of the kind, they would support legislation for Senate reform that might come to the Senate from this house.
Then he went on:
There was nothing in the nature of a written pledge. There was no pledge made to the government, as a government. It was an undertaking that was given to myself, as the one who was responsible for nominating members to the Senate. How many there were from whom I received that assurance. I cannot say at the present time. Nor am I in a position to say just when I ceased to raise that question. It did not become as important later on, when we had a majority in the Senate, and were in a position to see that permanent legislation originating in this house was not defeated because of action on the part of a hostile opposition in the upper chamber.
So I repeat that I believe the attitude of the late Mr. King, with regard to Senate


reform, was really only one of hypocrisy. Like the present Prime Minister, Mr. King kept quite a few vacancies all the time. I always believed he used them as a disciplinary measure. If there were eight vacancies in the Senate, there were at least ten Liberal aspirants for each of them. And while those vacancies remained not one of those ten would even draw a deep breath if he thought that would displease Mr. King. And it was a very-
Is that what happened in the first half of the thirties? Ask the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe.
I do not know.
It never bothered me.
There may have been a similar situation then, under the Conservative government, before I got here. I am speaking of what I have seen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You do not really believe that of any prime minister.

I do believe that of Mr. King, or I would not say it. Mr. King was a great political strategist, and he used vacancies in the Senate as one means of preserving discipline in the Liberal party.
The attitude of the present Prime Minister is different. I think his attitude to the Senate is one of utter indifference, and of hopelessness. He has more vacancies now, I believe -and a member of the government can correct me if I am wrong-than there have ever been since confederation, with an effect on public opinion which is disastrous so far as the Senate is concerned. If that is all the value the Prime Minister of this country places upon the Senate, why should any Canadian place more value upon it? Certainly it shows how little importance the Prime Minister places upon the other house.
He will get no one to take the vacancies, soon.

He showed very clearly his attitude toward the Senate last year during the discussion on the bill to increase salaries. I am referring to page 1639 of Hansard for February 1. During that debate several members brought up the question of Senate reform. They did not see why the senators should get the same increase as members of the House of Commons. The Prime Minister indicated quite tactfully that he did not see any reason either. He went on to say that if the members of the other house saw fit to amend that bill so they did not get as large an increase as the members of parliament, nobody here would feel very badly. But of course the senators did not rise to that suggestion very

quickly. They passed the bill through without any amendment in about half an hour, or certainly in less than an hour, and that was their answer to such a suggestion.
They were protecting the rights of the minorities.

Yes, perhaps that was one instance where they were protecting the rights of the minorities as they saw those rights, but here is the quotation that indicates the present Prime Minister's attitude toward the Senate. He approached the question on the basis of the constitution and said:
I must confess I have never felt that it was realistic to give any serious study or thought to the probability of modifying it. In order to modify it there would have to be also the concurrence of the members of the other house.
He was referring to the constitution as it related to the Senate. He went on:
Since I have been in Ottawa I have found that there were plenty of problems that it was realistic to study and consider, because I might have some responsibility in connection with forming some opinions as to the solutions they should receive.
As a matter of fact the Prime Minister has a lot of responsibility in this question of Senate reform, though he does not seem to recognize it. He went on:
I must confess I have never felt I was going to have in my day the responsibility of having to come to a conclusion about substantial modification as to the character of our constitution.
He should not have taken on the position of Prime Minister of Canada if he was not prepared to face this Senate problem, just as he had to face other problems. He went on:
I have heard certain modifications suggested about the way in which appointments on summonses to the other house might be made. But quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I have never heard one that did not seem to me to bristle with more obstacles than promises of advantage to the Canadian public.
That shows utter hopelessness with regard to reform of the Senate. I ask this question. Is the Prime Minister letting the Senate die out? Is he letting it fade away? Obviously he has not as yet shown any indication that he has given this problem any serious thought. If the statement he made on February 1 of last year reflects his attitude at the present time, there is not very much likelihood of reform of the Canadian Senate while the present Prime Minister holds his exalted position.
I do not blame the senators for the present position of the Senate. They are in reduced numbers. How can they possibly function properly when there are 22 vacancies, and no attempt whatever to fill them? It is recognized that appointments are for party service. Why should we try to camouflage the facts?
Proposed Senate Reform That is recognized here in the house today, and it is recognized in Canada from coast to coast. Twenty-eight or 29 of the present senators have been in the House of Commons as Liberal members since I came here in 1935. That is over one-third of the present Senate. I am not quarrelling with the fact that they are in the Senate. They deserve to be there just as much as anybody else who is there, but nearly everyone in the Senate has been either a member of this house, or in the provincial legislatures, or a defeated Liberal candidate, or has had some connection with active Liberal party organization.

I am not saying that the appointments made under Conservative prime ministers were always the correct ones. I am simply referring to the position of the Senate as we know it to be today, in 1955.
Furthermore, the Senate is given little important work to do. That of course is the fault of the government exclusively. Take legislation. During the present session we had a bill respecting the Canadian National Railways. It was a very important bill, bringing all the legislation having to do with the national railways together in one statute. That bill could very well have been introduced in the Senate. It was involved. It meant checking several dozen statutes, and the Senate could have done a thoroughly efficient job on that particular bill. Instead, it was introduced in the house when we were in a rush. Members of the house were very busy; and while we did the best job we could, this is one case where a bill could have been introduced in the Senate.
The same is true of the bill on the order paper now to amend the Transport Act, which has to do with agreed charges. It could have been initiated in the Senate, where again they could have given it more careful study than we can possibly do this week. It comes up in committee tomorrow. They could have called witnesses and made a thorough study of the bill.
This failure of the government to give the Senate very much real responsibility for initiating legislation has caused the more aggressive Senators to make their own business. I need only refer to Senator Crerar and his committee on finance, which has done a wonderful job for more than one year, and the committee under Senator Reid dealing with the traffic in narcotic drugs in Canada. These were cases where those particular senators made work for themselves and in so doing rendered a service to the people of the country.

I should like to point out that senators themselves during this session have debated this question of the failure to fill vacancies. Many of them have deprecated the fact that vacancies have continued for such a long period. The sum and substance of this part of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, is that the Senate has not been given a chance by the government. It is no wonder the Senate has ceased to command the serious attention of the country.
1 do suggest that some steps which might be taken to investigate this problem include first of all, as mentioned in the amendment, the method of appointment. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) suggested that men and women who are leaders in certain fields in Canada should be appointed to the Senate. I had intended to refer to men who are leaders in the labour field, in organized agricultural activities, in the universities of Canada and in the field of journalism, to mention only a few of the groups from which representatives should be appointed who would give great service to Canada in the Senate.
Then I believe this question of having senators appointed by the provincial governments is worthy of consideration. One of the main functions of the Senate is to protect the provinces, and surely it would help if a certain percentage of the senators were appointed by the provincial governments. Then on the tenure of office, to me the present provision has always seemed one of the indications that the fathers of confederation were only human. They were not perfect. When they arranged for tenure of office in the Senate they slipped up pretty badly. This very fact that a person is appointed for life means, because of the frailties of human nature, that a certain percentage of the members of the Senate can never function physically because they are too old. They are appointed for life and when they become ill and unable to carry on, they still occupy Senate seats. The result is that it is impossible to have the Senate function on the basis of all members being physically able to carry on.
Suggestions have been made that the appointments should be for a period of years, and ten years has been suggested. There would then be reappointments, and there has also been the further suggestion of compulsory retirement. Many years ago a leading public man suggested retirement at 80 years of age. I would not suggest that age today, but these are questions which we believe should be considered.
Consideration should also be given to making the Senate an elective body. I realize the reason the fathers of confederation made


it an appointed body was that they were thinking largely of British precedent, where they had lords in the House of Lords. We do not have any lords in this country, except that sometimes cabinet ministers think they are pretty near to being lords. The system here is different, and I believe a lot can be said for the elective system. Certainly there should be an investigation into that possibility. If the members of the Senate were elected they would fill a far more important place in the public life of the country than they do at the present time.
My final suggestion is that consideration should be given to finding ways and means of bringing about in the Senate more concern for the ordinary Canadian. I do not believe the ordinary Canadian has much chance under the present Senate set-up. Things have reached the stage under present conditions where the people from coast to coast who keep this country going, the men and women who are carrying the responsibilities of the country and without whom there would be no Canada, find it hard to get their problems before the Senate for consideration. In my opinion that is one of the great drawbacks to the present Senate set-up.
Above all there should be a recognition that there is a Senate problem and that something should be done about it. It looks as though the government is prepared just to sit out this debate and then vote down the amendment without attempting to justify the present position. Surely no one here would say that the present situation in the Senate is satisfactory. Other commonwealth countries which have been faced with this condition have taken steps to bring about changes and make their upper houses more in line with reality.
Since I came here in 1935 I have seen the Senate decline steadily, more particularly in recent years. When I came here first, senators prided themselves on their non-partisanship, and I am referring now to senators representing both parties. I ran into that on more than one occasion, but now there is nothing left about which they can pride themselves. Certainly there is very little political independence left in the other house.

I would ask the hon. member to use as great care as possible in referring to the other house. I have been worried since this debate was initiated because of what has been said, which might be taken as rather offensive as far as the other place is concerned. If you wish I shall withdraw that remark. In conclusion may I say that the solution for this problem can come only from the Prime Minister. No one else can give a lead in facing up to and settling this problem. He has the greatest majority that any Prime Minister of Canada has ever had, both in the House of Commons and in the Senate.
