The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, as we all know the Senate is supposed to fulfil certain definite functions. It was originally conceived as a body of outstanding, knowledgeable and public-spirited Canadians who were to gather together and deliberate on the measures passed by this House of Commons. I think we would all agree that many of the members of the present Senate are men who have served their country in the finest way possible, as senior statesmen, and have made a great contribution to the legislation of this country. Their advice has been widely sought, and they have brought outstanding ability to bear on the deliberations of our affairs.
However, I think it is highly unfortunate that right from the beginning the Senate has been appointed by the government of the day. For that reason, irrespective of what party happened to form the government, the Senate became largely a lush pasture for the supporters of the party which happened to be in power at that time. Many senators today, I believe, have been appointed-and this is no change from the past-because they were quite candidly faithful party members whom the government believed it should reward for some reason or other; or were members of the House of Commons whom the party in power found impossible to regulate here in this chamber, and so they were moved upstairs.
Latterly, because we have had one party in power in this country for the past 20 years, the Senate really has become a retirement haven for faithful Liberal party workers or members, instead of being what it was originally intended to be, namely a gathering of the best minds in the country to discuss and instigate legislation without being subject to the influences and pressures which are brought to bear upon members of
Proposed Senate Reform the House of Commons by those who send us here, and in that way be able to give clear judgment on the issues brought before them.
I think we would all agree, and I know it is the feeling of the people of the country, that because of the particular set-up of the Senate at the present time, with all but seven members coming from one party, the Senate today is no more nor less than a rubber stamp for the government.
In days gone by the Senate was represented on a fairly even basis, with the membership divided between the two old parties; but now, as I say, all but seven come from one party. I think we would all agree, and I feel sure that the government does so, that this is not a good thing for any legislative body. The Prime Minister today has the opportunity to make this a body of legislators which can regain the confidence of the people of Canada and restore the Senate to its real place and its real authority. Senators do not need to have political affiliations, but they should have great and wide experience and ideas which they can bring to bear on the discussions in which they take part.
As has been suggested by other members who have spoken in the debate today, I believe we should have many more outstanding representatives from various fields of endeavour in this country. To mention six fields only, I feel the Senate should have outstanding representatives from the fields of industrial management, labour, agriculture, education, science and culture. If appointments were made from those ranks in the future, I believe the Senate would be immeasurably strengthened. In fact I believe appointments of that kind must be made in future or the demand by the people of Canada for the abolition of the Senate will eventually become stronger than any government can withstand and abolition would take place.
I believe it would be a sorry state of affairs to have that happen. I think a group of men and women who are not obliged to face the electorate every four or five years, as do the elected representatives in the House of Commons, could view legislation in a much more impartial manner because they would be unswayed by the problems which were facing the people who sent them here, and could form more objective judgments on the problems that our country is facing today.
Such a group would have the time in which to really contemplate the issues of the day. They would have no axes to grind. They could bring fresh viewpoints to bear and

Proposed Senate Reform could introduce amendments to our legislation which I think would be very constructive indeed.
I believe that was the true function for which the Senate was originally intended and the real reason it is part of our Canadian constitution. I think we should make our Senate one composed of members who can fulfil this function of objective deliberation.
If that function is carried out, I believe the role of the Senate can be restored to that which was originally intended. As has been said today, the Prime Minister has a wonderful opportunity to bring the Senate back to life and to it restore the esteem to which I believe it is entitled. Today there are 18 vacancies. The Prime Minister I know will agree that-
There are 22 vacancies.
Twenty-two?
Yes; you are out of date.

That shows how quickly these things move along. Perhaps the figure will be 23 tomorrow and 24 the next day. That is all the more reason for taking this action. I believe the Prime Minister would agree that to appoint 22 more members of the Liberal party to the Senate, persons who are Liberal supporters-although that has been the practice followed by both parties in the past-would simply make the Senate even more ridiculous, as far as being an impartial body is concerned, than people already consider it to be.
I feel the Prime Minister has a wonderful opportunity to choose outstanding representatives in the fields I have mentioned, namely those of industrial management, agriculture, labour, education, science and culture. I believe those people could bring tremendous knowledge to bear on the discussions in the Senate, and could restore it to its proper place. As further vacancies occurred more men and more women of this calibre could be added, and in that way I think the legislative procedures of parliament would be immeasurably improved.
I know the Prime Minister does not have an easy choice in this matter. I really feel that he agrees with what I have said. These are not new ideas; they are old ones. I really feel that in what I have said he agrees with me. I also sympathize with him because of the problem he is up against. I know and he knows that as soon as he announced a policy of this kind the telephones would be ringing, the wires would be clogged and the mails would be jammed with violent protests from thousands of faithful

Liberal party members, all of whom think they are in line for one of these 22 vacancies.
I know the problems the Prime Minister would face, but I think he is a big enough man to face them. I hope he will do so, because it is the only chance we have of restoring the Senate to the position of respect to which it is entitled in the minds of the Canadian people. If something of that kind is not done I think the demand of the people will be that the Senate be abolished, because I believe they will feel that it is ridiculous to pay out large sums of money to operate the Senate if the Senate obviously is not able to pass impartial judgment on the legislation passed by this house, and for that reason has no real function in our parliament today.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a few brief words. I think I can consistently make a few corrections, because I am not looking for an appointment to the Senate. Personally I do not think the hon. member who introduced this question and those who have spoken on it are seeking reform now, because they know perfectly well that if they had wanted reform they would have brought up the question at the beginning of the session, not now when it is impossible to introduce legislation. Therefore I think they are wide of the mark.
We brought it up in 1950.

Second, a number of hon. members of the opposition think the Senate is at a low ebb. At supper time I heard somebody say, "Hurrah for the Senate". I do not think the Senate has ever been better than it is at the present time. It is all right to hit at somebody because you think it is popular to hit at them, but even the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said that the former member for New Westminster, Senator Reid, has done work that has been highly commended. Never since I came here has the Senate had so much front page publicity. Some members have said there should be an age limit. Why have an age limit in the Senate when there is no age limit here?
Because your constituents can decide.

I am not 75. When you tell me I cannot be a member of the House of Commons, tell the citizens of Fort William and they will talk to you. It is all right talking to people who are far away and cannot reply. I think the Senate have done a fine job.
The Senate occupies the position of a court. I know some of its members who were once

members of the House of Commons. When they were here they were just as efficient as anybody in the house, and they have not changed a bit. I have listened to them a few times when there were some dry speeches going on here. I slipped over there to hear something excellent, and I did. It is all right to blame the people on the other side of the house, but I am convinced that today the Senate is doing a better job than it has ever done since I came here.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker; that is all I have to say.

Mr. Speaker, the policy of my party with respect to the Senate is that it should be abolished and of course I am in favour of that policy, though I must admit I never could get very enthusiastic about it because I could never see clearly how we would set about to abolish the Senate. I felt that if we formed the government the first thing we would have to do would be to get somebody in the Senate to represent us there, even at the opening of parliament, and once having embarked on that course we probably might consider changing our policy of abolition.
It is rather strange that at this time we should hear so much talk about restoring the Senate to its former place in the government of the country. If the Senate has fallen from its former place of usefulness in the governmental set-up of the nation, surely there must be some reason for that. I do not think the reason can be that the present Prime Minister is not filling the vacancies fast enough. I imagine if the Prime Minister felt he needed to have more representatives in the Senate he would fill the vacancies very quickly.
As for myself, I do not think it would make a particle of difference to the other place, to this house or to the country at large if 22 new members were appointed to the Senate. You cannot get anything more from the Senate than you are getting from it now. It has become the fifth wheel on the governmental machine, and in my opinion it is really no use to try to restore that wheel to usefulness by attaching some sort of power to it, putting a new tire on it or any of the other things that one does with a wheel.

What would the Senate do that is not already being done by this chamber, a chamber elected by the people of Canada to do the things the people of Canada want done? It has been said that the Senate should be made more useful and given more
Proposed Senate Reform power, but remember that the Senate in its present form has the same powers as this chamber except in one small particular. It has the power to veto what has been done here by those who were democratically elected to govern the country.
Oh, I don't care what you say, Angus.

There goes one man who cannot stand to hear the truth. In my opinion a non-elected Senate that has the power of veto over an elected chamber is the negation of democracy. Not only is that so, but in all countries today where they have the parliamentary system the tendency is toward a one-chamber parliament. In New Zealand the Senate was abolished a few years ago. Who abolished it? The Conservatives, when they came into office. The second chamber in the United Kingdom, the mother of parliaments, has been brought to a position where it is practically absolutely useless as a legislative body.
Have we, the elected members of the House of Commons, so little faith in our own capacity to deal with matters affecting Canada that come before us that we must have them reviewed by a non-elected body of men who can say to us, "Go and play marbles; we know what the people want and you do not".
It is said that the function of the Senate when Canada became a nation was to protect the interests of minorities. I never saw it in print, but I am told that Sir John A. Macdonald said that was the function of the Senate, to protect the interests of the rich who were always in the minority.
He did not put it that way.
I do not know whether he said it better or worse than that.
He said he would protect minorities, and as the rich were often in the minority they might as well be protected too.
My informant is just as good as the one I am hearing now.
Yours has the new socialist look.

What Sir John A. Macdonald said was that its function was to protect minorities, and as the rich were always in the minority its function was to protect the rich. It has done that pretty well.
I appreciate that the Prime Minister has a problem. His predecessor had a problem, but I think for his predecessor the problem was easier than it is for the present Prime
5346	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform Minister. I do not like to speak disrespectfully of one who has departed, but I think the former prime minister was more of a cynic than the present one. He felt he had reformed the Senate sufficiently when he had a majority of Liberals there. He never made any further attempt to reform it after that. As a matter of fact, I believe he gave up asking questions of those who were being appointed when he was getting to the position where, in the natural order of things, he could have a majority in the Senate without making any promises or accepting any.
I do not care for many of the proposals that have been made here regarding the Senate. If we are going to have a Senate in a democratic country I believe that Senate should be elected. As I said before I am not afraid to discuss any problem, and I think I can discuss any subject objectively. There is a feeling that we discuss problems and take action on problems because we are elected members, which we would not do if we did not have to seek election. Surely if there is anyone in that position in this house he should not be here. A person who cannot face the electorate and tell them, "I favour this because I think it is for the benefit of Canada", or "I do not favour that because I do not think it is for the benefit of Canada", has no right to be here. I am not going to advocate something because some few people think we ought to have it and I cannot find it in my heart to say no.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre had a proposal for reforming the Senate by appointing a labour man to it. Well, the Senate will not be reformed by appointing one labour man to it: that is not what I would call labour representation in the Senate. In order to give labour the representation it ought to have in the Senate it should have members in the Senate approximately equal to labour's voting strength in the country. Labour will not be represented by the appointment of one old man who has retired from other fields of endeavour in the labour movement. We want young men in the Senate if the Senate is going to be useful.
I see the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) shakes his head. Perhaps he does not want young men in the Senate. Perhaps the government does not want young men in the Senate. But the people of this country want young men in the Senate if they want a Senate that is going to be of any use.
We fill the other place with old gentlemen who have retired or are about to retire from whatever useful work they were doing. As a matter of fact they were retired from the world. Then we expect these old gentlemen to
[Mr. Maclnnis.j

give a 1955 or 1956 expression of opinion on the problems that affect Canada. What utter nonsense! They cannot think in terms of 1955 or 1956; they think in terms of the years of their activity. That is not the kind of Senate I want.
Then again, I do not think it would be desirable to have the provinces appoint certain members to the other place. I believe it would make for all kinds of trouble. We come here to this parliament to represent Canada, not Quebec, British Columbia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and so on. I said we would get into all kinds of trouble. We will vote for this amendment. Because the Senate is a problem child so far as Canada is concerned I suppose something has to be done with it. At the moment it is fairly harmless, and it is a good divorce court.
I think it would be desirable to discuss what we should do with the Senate, or what place it ought to hold in the government of Canada. For that reason we believe, as has already been stated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, this amendment is in order and it would bring about that result. It is a question worthy of discussion, but let us think of it objectively. Sometime we may have to abolish it, but I think one of the great difficulties in the way of abolishing the Canadian Senate is that it cannot be abolished without its own consent.
I am not a constitutional expert or anything like that, but I find now that we have to go to the imperial parliament for certain amendments to the British North America Act. There are certain amendments with which we have power to deal ourselves, but I doubt very much if this chamber, on its own resolution, could get the imperial parliament to abolish the Senate. I think we would very likely have to have the consent of both houses of parliament.
After what has been said, I thought I had better say these few words in regard to the other place, whether or not you agree with them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I be allowed to say that in participating in the debate hon. members should not indulge in expressions which might imply some reflection upon members of the other house. I refer to Bourinot's fourth edition, page 360:
In the House of Commons a member will not be permitted by the Speaker to indulge in any reflections on the house itself as a political institution, or as a branch of the government or upon the other house; or to impute to any member or members unworthy motives for their actions in a particular case; or to use any profane or indecent language, such as is unfit for the house to hear or for any member to utter; or to question the acknowledged and undoubted powers of the house

in a matter of privilege; or to reflect upon, argue against or in any manner call in question, the past acts and proceedings of the house-
I would ask hon. members, while they are discussing reform of the Senate, to be very careful as to the expressions they use with respect to the other house.

This amendment deals with a matter that I feel is of continuing interest and has been debated over the years. Invariably during the course of those debates on this subject strong expressions have been used regarding the Senate and the membership of the Senate.
I do not intend to indulge in that type of discussion. But I would point out to you, sir, that no one ever spoke in stronger and more uncontrolled language regarding the Senate than did the late prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King. I should like on this occasion to make one or two suggestions, particularly because I believe that this is a subject of inherent interest to the people of Canada and to the preservation of democracy under our system of government.
It is hard to understand why one of the co-equal partners in the government of this country should have been treated, as it has been in the last several years, with an almost undisguised contempt by the government of Canada. Either the Senate performs the functions and responsibilities envisaged by the fathers of confederation, or it is a useless institution. I am one of those who believe the Senate is necessary to the constitutional preservation of the rights of minorities in this country. That was its original concept; that was the idea of the fathers of confederation; that was the basis upon which the several provinces which entered confederation accepted it. Without that basis those provinces would not have entered.
It is interesting to study the general concept lying behind the necessity for a second chamber. Going back to the days prior to the rebellion of 1837 one finds that one of the major reasons for that civil war was the fact that there was a legislative council not responsible in any way to the people but, under the colonial system then prevailing, almost all-powerful in its relationship to the elected chamber. And it is interesting to trace what happened following the rebellion of 1837. Under the act of union provision was made for a legislative council and for an assembly, the legislative council to be appointed by the governor. Under that system every councillor was appointed for life. Upper and Lower Canada had an equal number of members. The total had no maximum, but the minimum was fixed at 20.
Proposed Senate Reform
Complaints arose that an appointed legislative council was not in keeping with responsible government, so in 1854, by a statute of the legislature of Canada, power was given to elect the members of the legislative council. In 1856 the government of the day brought in the legislation making provision for the elected or appointed legislative council, as the case might be, with 24 representatives from Upper Canada and 24 from Lower Canada. The term in the case of those elected was eight years, with one-quarter retiring every two years.
When the conference took place at Charlottetown, and the later one at Quebec, on the basis of the experience the representatives of the people had had in connection with an elected upper chamber they were agreed on one thing. That was that the upper chamber was necessary to preserve the rights of minorities, and that it could not be an elected body, for otherwise it would ultimately become the all-powerful legislative body.
Facing this problem today we agree on one thing. That is, whether we believe confederation was a pact or that the statute of confederation was a statute, the basis of confederation, or the reason certain of the provinces gave up their rights, was on the sure foundation that there would be two chambers in this country, one appointed and the other elected.
While it is interesting to speculate as to whether or not the Senate could be abolished by an amendment passed by the House of Commons and the Senate

 and I believe it could, without any resort to Westminster, provided there was in fact a majority in the Senate desirous of achieving the execution of that body-it is my personal belief that it would be the derogation of one of the major constitutional foundations upon which confederation was built. Therefore I do not go with those who believe we should end the Senate, but I do believe that the responsibility facing people today, and in particular facing this parliament, is that it should do its part- if I may use a phrase of Dr. R. A. MacKay -not to end but to mend the Senate.
When I hear some hon. gentlemen say the Senate has not discharged any of its responsibilities, again I do not belong to that school. On occasions over the years it has been a block to legislation passed in the House of Commons. But, with the perspective of history, as one looks back with an appreciation of events as he reviews the past, it becomes clear that on a number of occasions the Senate has been right in the action it has taken. When I hear some criticizing the Senate because of the manner in which it
5348	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform discharges its responsibilities with respect to divorce, I must say that personally I am among those who believe that the attention given by the Senate and its committee to divorce proceedings coming before them is such that the cases receive as fair, as considerate and as deliberative consideration as is given by the courts of law.
I have never dealt with this divorce question before. In the 15 years I have been in the House of Commons I have heard the Senate condemned and maligned for its failure properly to examine the divorce cases coming before it. Making due allowance for the frailties of human nature, and the errors made as well in the courts of law, I feel the Senate does in fact discharge its responsibilities in connection with divorce in a manner that assures, in large measure, a degree of just conclusions at least equal to that which can be expected in the courts of law.
Having said that, however, I do believe the attitude taken by the Prime Minister toward the Senate in the last few years is difficult to understand. After all, it is his prerogative and privilege to make appointments to the Senate. The general concept of confederation was that these appointments were his. And while in the experience of history the minister or ministers from any province could have consideration given to their views, the fact remains that under the general plan of confederation these appointments were indeed the responsibility of the prime minister.
The reason given for this at the time of the discussions in Charlottetown and Quebec was in fact this, that the prime minister would endeavour in the appointments made to assure the maintenance of the highest degree of legislative responsibility and competence in that body.
I cannot understand, and certainly the people of Canada have difficulty understanding, why a body composed of such responsible and able people as the Senate should be placed in the position that it functions with only partial representation. It might be said that we are saving money by not making these appointments. If that be so, Mr. Speaker, we could save a great deal more by abolishing the institution altogether. But as long as the Senate exists there can be no justification for delays in appointments of the duration that has been the case in recent years.
There are 22 vacancies. Five have existed for two years, three for four years, five for five years and one for six years. Either the Prime Minister has some faith in this institution and intends to wait until a sufficient number die so he may be able to put an
TMr. Diefenbaker.]

even greater majority in the Senate and thereby reform it; or, on the other hand, it reveals an undisguised contempt for an institution which I believe is deserving of better consideration from the government of the day.
I believe the Senate is necessary. I do not know what are the Prime Minister's views on the British North America Act, whether he regards it as a pact as did one or two of the fathers of confederation and as did the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, who on more than one occasion in this house definitely stated that in his opinion it was a pact. He referred to it as such on March 9, 1927. He said, "It is indeed a pact." I notice that Dr. MacKay in his book "The Unreformed Senate of Canada" takes the stand that morally it is a compact among the provinces of Canada. Whether it is that or not, it was an agreement, and the Senate was a necessary and requisite part of that agreement.
That being so, I believe it should be the earnest endeavour of the government of the day to ensure that the Senate shall have its membership filled within a reasonable time, instead of placing the Senate in the position where it is in the nature of hope deferred, or the dangling of a carrot before the eyes of those within the Liberal party who hope that time will ultimately assure their elevation to that body.
Where are the reform promises of the old days? Will the Prime Minister tell the house what happened to all those carefully drawn agreements during the 1920's? The late Mr. King went to the country twice on a policy of reform of the Senate. He contended that the means whereby that reform would be effected would be through the instrumentality of the executioners appointed by him to the Senate.
Mention was made this afternoon by my hon. friend the Acting Leader of the Opposition that in 1927 John Evans, then the member for Rosetown, asked Mr. King this question, as reported at page 355 of Hansard:
What is the form or wording of the pledge, if any, taken from those who have been appointed senators during the last two years with a view to Senate reform? How many have been thus pledged?
Mr. King answered:
An assurance of support of such measure of Senate reform, in conformity with the requirements of the constitution, as may be introduced by the Liberal administration.
This assurance has been given by all who have accepted appointment to the Senate within the time mentioned.
I have not gone to the trouble to ascertain how many went into the Senate on the basis

of this plan. The Prime Minister should be able to tell the house and the country whether a similar plan is in existence today, and whether in the appointments that have been made since he became Prime Minister of this country an undertaking was secured.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can tell the hon. gentleman at once that I have never made any condition whatsoever with any gentleman whom I recommended to the governor for appointment to the Senate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What about the ladies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I never asked any persons whose names I submitted for summons to the Senate to make any commitment whatsoever as to how they would discharge their responsibilities in their legislative capacity.

That clarifies the issue. I am surprised to see some of my hon. friends applauding that statement for at one time some of them were applauding the late Mr. King when he mentioned this pledge, this assurance. It surprises me to learn that in recent days the point of view has changed. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, if the late Mackenzie King could hear what has taken place here this evening or even be communicated with in this regard I am sure he would feel deeply shocked at the departure from those principles for which the Liberal party stood for so long.
I do not think he would.

I was not going to bring my hon. friend into it, but the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is in a peculiarly good position to tell us, both on past and present knowledge, when it was that Mr. Mackenzie-King departed from that great and abiding principle, the assurance from all the appointees to the Senate that whenever they achieved a majority they would indeed reform themselves.
I shall be glad to tell the hon. gentleman. Mr. King did say to me on one occasion that all public men sometimes had to change their minds.

Well, that is a reasonable statement coming from the gentleman who has established a reputation in that regard unequalled in this country. It is a strange thing, though, that Mr. King should have changed his mind after having been successful in two elections on the basis of a promise that apparently was never intended to be carried into effect.
I do say, Mr. Speaker, it is helpful that the house has in its ranks one who was so close to the late right hon. gentleman, and
Proposed Senate Reform who is able to tell us at first hand exactly what ideas passed through the mind of Mr. King, and why it was he changed his mind so definitely after a promise had been made that had been singularly successful in winning elections. These are things on which the minister should be able to enlighten the house during the course of this debate.
I ask him, when he speaks, to tell the house when, if ever, Mr. King changed his mind regarding this great subject of Senate reform. When did he finally determine he had been wrong? When was it that this change of attitude took place? Because in 1925 and in 1926 reform of the Senate was of the essence of the platform upon which Mr. King and those associated with him sought power in this country.
Having said that, I should like to mention some alternative suggestions that have been made as to how the Senate could be reformed. I do not have in mind recommending the appointment of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to the Senate, but he certainly could bring light to the Senate regarding the whole problem if he were to be appointed there.
Different suggestions for the reform of the Senate have been made over the years. First, there has been the suggestion of an elective senate, but that generally is unacceptable. The experience of the United States has been that with a senate elected for a longer period than the House of Representatives, the Senate has become an all-powerful institution. It was never intended by the fathers of confederation that our parliamentary system should be different in principle from the British; therefore an elective senate seems to be out of the question.
The matter was dealt with at considerable length in 1923 by the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. Mr. Fielding had the advantage of being acquainted with many of the fathers of confederation. In addition he had had long experience as premier of the province of Nova Scotia, and as a minister in the federal cabinet. His contention was that the constitution of the Senate was not satisfactory. That was his considered opinion as given to the house on March 31, 1923, beginning at page 1375 of Hansard. He did not believe it should be abolished, but felt that it should be a brake and not a block on the House of Commons. He suggested that the tenures of the senators then in office should not be disturbed, and felt that there should be a recognition of provincial rights by having certain appointments made after consultation with the provincial governments. He was opposed to an elective senate, and he concluded by saying that the surest means of
5350	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform making the Senate an effective legislative body was to have the appointments for ten years with provision for reappointment for a further period of ten years.
These views of Mr. Fielding, representing as they do the essence of his experience, indicate some of the problems that could and should be considered by the government of the day, and would be considered if effect were given to this amendment.
All of us represent the opinions, reasonable and authoritative as they are, of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Mac-Innis). But I was rather surprised to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) applauded the hon. member when he stated there was no justification for a second chamber with power and authority to veto the acts of the representatives of the people. The Minister of Finance applauded that statement. If his applause meant his concurrence, then there is every indication that there is need to reform the Senate. Personally I disagree with that viewpoint. I think for the House of Commons or for parliament to take the stand that there should be a senate but that the senate should have no power to act on sober second thought would be a denial of the principles and basis of confederation.
Of veto?

Veto? It is not in reality a veto. What the hon. member is talking about is not a veto. The Senate may defeat legislation; but there is no senate today, following the experience during the days of Lloyd George in the historic House of Lords debates of 1910 and 1911, that would continue to turn down legislation passed by the House of Commons should the House of Commons be dissolved and the people return the government that introduced the legislation that had been turned down at an earlier session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is not that just another way of saying what was said over there?

Oh, no. There is no case I know of wherein legislation has been turned down repeatedly, or turned down following an election where the government had gone to the country and asked for a mandate from the people. The only veto power is that provided for under the constitution. I ask the Minister of Finance whether it is his considered opinion that some change should be made in this regard, and that the Senate should not have the power of giving reconsideration to hasty and ill-digested legislation passed by the House of Commons.
These are but some of the problems immediately suggesting themselves. For these reasons I believe the country as a whole


would support the government giving consideration to initiating the necessary consultation and inquiry respecting reform of the Senate so that all appropriate steps may be taken to ensure that the Senate may effectively discharge its constitutional functions as an integral part of our parliamentary system.
Having regard to the events of the last few years, during which the Senate has been deliberately sidetracked and allowed to operate with three wheels rather than the four provided for under the constitution, I feel that the Canadian people have the right to ask the Prime Minister to place before the house and the country the reasons vacancies have been allowed to continue in the other body. As I said a moment ago, there have been one for six years, five for five years, three for four years and five for two years. Either the Senate has a function to perform and the government wants to see that function performed, or the purpose of allowing these vacancies to continue is to provide that when a sufficient number of vacancies exists, action will be taken similar to that taken by Prime Minister Holland in New Zealand, when appointments were made of a body of appointed, self-dedicated executioners who themselves voted their legislative council out of existence.
Someone may say that the reform of the Senate is a theoretical matter. There is nothing very theoretical in asking that the institutions of our democracy be made effective. How can any institution be effective if its membership is allowed to remain one-quarter unfilled? What kind of House of Commons would we have if vacancies were allowed to remain unfilled for one, two, three or four years? After all, the Senate has an equal responsibility with the House of Commons in the passing of legislation. It is Her Majesty the Queen on the advice of the Senate and the House of Commons; that is the way we are constituted to legislate for this country. The Senate is over there sitting between times emasculated in its membership, with no power to improve its position and having but one recourse, appointments by the Prime Minister to fill the vacancies.
The Prime Minister having now assured the house and the country that those who are appointed to the Senate go there without any strings attached, I suggest that he now let us in on the secret as to why these vacancies have been allowed to continue so long, and possibly even restore some degree of hope to some of my hon. friends opposite who have been waiting for a long time in the expectant hope of being elevated to that body.

I suggest that the Prime Minister should tell the house and the country how anyone can expect a senate to be effective and efficient and properly to discharge its democratic duty with three-quarters of its membership there and one-quarter unappointed, some for several years and many for two and three years.

Mr. Speaker, the question of Senate reform is not a new subject in this house. Even in the few years I have been here I have heard it discussed on numerous occasions. I have never expressed an opinion on the matter myself, but I have a few thoughts that I should like to present today.
First of all, a great deal of discussion has centred around the question of whether there should be a senate as such and whether, if it is to be reformed, it should be an elected rather than an appointed body. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway proposed what in my opinion was a serious and thought-provoking question, when he stated that a constitutional difficulty would be involved in asking this chamber to pass legislation abolishing another part of this parliament which eventually would have to pass through the other place. In effect it would be asking the Senate to pass a bill to abolish themselves. One can foresee some difficulty there.
I think the real difficulty lies in the fact that any major move to reform or to abolish any part of this parliament would involve the Canadian constitution. Since it does that it actually involves more than the members of this house or the members of the other place. It involves all the people of Canada.
In most democratic countries the method that has been used to bring about a major change in a constitution has been what is known as the constituent assembly, which is chosen for that specific purpose and, having fulfilled that purpose, is disbanded and is no more. There may be some practical difficulties in doing that in our own country. Perhaps the closest thing that could be found in Canada is the dominion-provincial conference, which is held now and then in order to iron out the difficulties that may arise as between the jurisdiction of the provinces and that of the federal government; but I believe perhaps the best method of all would be to test public opinion on this question, because even at a dominion-provincial conference I think it could be argued by both the federal and the provincial representatives that neither had a clear mandate from the people they represent to bring about a major change in the Canadian constitution on this point.
Proposed Senate Reform Perhaps as a way of testing public opinion directly and specifically on that question a plebiscite might prove to be the best method. If such a plebiscite were arranged for, I suggest that it would at the same time do away with the difficulty of having to ask the other place to pass legislation to which they may at the present time be opposed; because, before such a plebiscite could be held, legislation would have to be passed both in this chamber and in the other chamber to provide for the plebiscite. If such legislation received the approval of both houses, then if not legally at least morally, both houses would be bound to accept the verdict of the plebiscite.
In holding a plebiscite there is always the question of what should be submitted to the public. I would suggest that three questions could be asked. The first perhaps could be this: Are you in favour of the abolition of the Senate? The second could be: If not, are you in favour of an elected senate rather than an appointed one, the elections to be held on a provincial basis, with so many for each province to be elected? And the third, of course, would be the obvious one: If you are not in favour of the first two, are you in favour of leaving the Senate as it is?
I believe if they were given a specific opportunity to express themselves on that question, we would be given a clear indication of what the people of Canada really think about this extremely important question; and it is important because, as I said, it involves the constitution of Canada. That is my suggestion as to how it could be carried out.
Of course if this motion which is now before us were carried I would imagine that, under even the terms of this amendment, the government could proceed to make plans for the very thing I have suggested. But I have been around this place long enough to realize that the chances of this amendment carrying are rather slim, to say the least, and that after it has been disposed of we shall likely still be faced with the status quo and still have the same situation as before. That being so, and the chances being that we shall still have a senate constituted in much the same way it is now constituted, for some considerable period of time, I should like to make a few suggestions as to appointments to the Senate.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre in his address today referred to the fact that one of the functions of the Senate is, as he stated, to protect minority rights. I should like to put it in a slightly different way. I do not particularly like the term "protect minority rights", because it almost indicates that those minority rights are under

Proposed Senate Reform attack and need protection. I state this as my considered opinion. I doubt whether there is any democratic country in the world in which minority rights are less under attack than they are in our own country. It is not so much a matter of protecting minority rights as it is a matter of doing the democratic thing, and that is to see that all so-called minorities are represented to the greatest extent possible in the Senate chamber.
I say "so-called minorities" because, as a matter of fact, in Canada we are in a rather curious position in that all people, with respect to their ethnic origins, are in a minority; and at the same time we are all in a majority. That statement may sound rather Irish, but it is a fact. If we look at the latest vital statistics, for 1951, according to the Canada Year Book we find that out of a total at that time of about 14 million people there were roughly, just in round numbers,
6.700.000	of British origin and 4,300,000 of French origin; then there were 619,000 of German origin, 395,000 of Ukrainian origin,
264.000	of Netherlands origin, 219,000 of Polish origin, 189,000 of Jewish origin, 152,000 of Italian origin and 119,000 of Norwegian origin.
I have taken only those groups in which there were over 100,000. There were many more categories that could be named. When one adds those figures and takes off a few percentages, one finds that no ethnic group in Canada at the present time is an absolute majority. As a matter of fact, every ethnic group in Canada is a minority, but from another point of view we are all in the majority. We sometimes talk about minority rights, language rights, religious rights and so on, as if only the minority concerned had the right to speak the particular language or follow the particular faith. As a matter of fact there is no restriction upon anyone in Canada speaking any language or practising any religious faith he desires. From that point of view we are all in the majority, because we are free to exercise the minority rights that all the minorities themselves can practise.
Then there is one very important group, though not a particularly large one, which I have not yet mentioned. I refer to our Indian and Eskimo population of 165,000. I have put these statistics on the record for this reason. As I have stated, it is not a question of protecting minority rights because they are certainly not under attack by anyone in Canada, but I believe it is desirable in a democratic system to have our governmental bodies represent, as far as possible, a true cross-section of the people who are governed.


There are two kinds of government positions. One kind is an elected position such as members of the House of Commons and of provincial legislatures occupy. So far as elected positions are concerned, it is up to the people themselves through their own efforts, ingenuity, activity and energy to see to it that they have the kind of representation they desire. There is nothing either this parliament or the government of Canada can dc* about that. It is purely a matter of the public looking after their own interests.
But appointed positions are in a different category, because they are taken out of the hands of the general public, who have no say as to who should be appointed to various positions. That is the prerogative and responsibility of the government. It so happens that one of these responsibilities is that of appointments to the Senate. I therefore suggest that if we are going to make an effort to see that all minorities are represented in so far as it is physically practical and possible to do so, a little attention should be paid the fact that more than 20 per cent of the people of Canada are of neither British nor French origin.
I mention this as a statistical fact and as a reminder that when we talk about minorities we are talking about a great variety of people in Canada, and it might be desirable to take into consideration the fact that at the present time this group of over 20 per cent of our population are not, so far as I know, represented in the Senate. I suggest that when the government are making appointments to the Senate they should look around for suitable, qualified persons who could be considered as representative of that sector of the Canadian population.
I am not aware how many of these various ethnic groups have made representations. I know one particular group has brought this matter to the attention of the government, and no doubt others have also done so. I hope their representations are being given serious consideration, and that some action will follow in the near future.
I want to say a particular word about one group who in my opinion have a special claim to representation. I refer to the Indian and Eskimo population of 165,000. So far as the Indian population are concerned, their status has changed to some extent in recent years due to the fact that in all the provinces of Canada they have been given the right of franchise in provincial elections with no strings attached whatever. They have also been allowed to vote in federal elections, with the stipulation that they must sign a waiver so far as income tax is concerned. In other words they are coming closer and closer to

enjoying the full privileges and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
There are good reasons why it is going to be difficult for some time yet for these people to become sufficiently organized to have representation in this house. One difficulty is the way in which they live and the regions in which they live. I think a very good case can be made why the Indian population should have a representative in the Senate to look after their widespread and often complicated interests. If any group has a claim to prior rights, certainly they are among those who have such a claim.
In placing these considerations before the house I want to make it quite clear that in naming these various ethnic groups I am not picking or choosing, and am not making a plea for any particular group. But I believe it is only fair and reasonable that when we speak of having minority representation in the Senate-not particularly in the interests of protecting minority rights because, as I said, they are not under attack-we should see to it that the voice of these people is heard along with that of other Canadians. In my opinion the appointment of one or more senators to represent that 20 per cent or more of our population would constitute an important reform and a step forward.

Mr. Speaker, I would not venture to ask the house to listen to me at this time of night on this subject if it were not that I believe it is a very important subject which is in danger of losing its importance in the eyes of the people. If there ever was a case of the old adage that familiarity breeds contempt it seems to me it has come to be very nearly true with regard to debates on the Senate.
Of course, to begin with they are not debates. Apparently the only contribution we are to have from the other side is from the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), and his speech seemed to me more like a hallelujah chorus than a contribution to a debate. I feel that the matter is treated as so many things are treated nowadays, with something verging on contempt. I do not like to use that word, but we saw that attitude the other day when we made the best arguments we could with regard to reviewing government methods of carrying on their business, and there was no reply at all.
I believe the question of the Senate is of great importance. I believe that the wise men who set it up knew what they were doing. I have done some work on the matter myself, and I think I have learned something. Although I am afraid it will be dull for those who are here, I propose to put on
Proposed Senate Reform the record some of the sayings of the wise and able men who thought this thing through, so that even if no one in this chamber has much interest in the matter these sayings will be on the record for the benefit of others who may possibly be interested. That is my excuse for asking the house to listen to me for some time, and I make no apology for it.
As I say, I think this is a matter of great importance which is being treated as if it were of little importance. Nobody suggests that this world is so easy and free from trouble that we are going to have no difficult problems in government. As a matter of fact the government have set up a royal commission for the purpose of assisting them in solving their problems, and I feel we should be reviewing our own institutions, our own organization, our own system of government and seeking in every way to improve it. I believe our treatment of the Senate stands out and is a sore spot.
I am not going to say a word disrespectful of the Senate. There are able men there, both older and younger. There are very able young men and there are men of ripe experience whose judgment is useful to us now. I shall content myself as far as that is concerned by referring to what the hon. member for Prince Albert has already said with respect to the disregard with which the Senate is treated. I would say one does not need to prove that there is a Senate problem. You do not need to prove it is a fine day when the sun is shining. You do not need to prove there is a problem when you hear it discussed whenever the Senate is mentioned. I shall just read a sentence from Professor MacKay's book, at page 206. His book has already been mentioned, "The Unreformed Senate of Canada". He says this:
Probably on no other public question in Canada has there been such unanimity of opinion as on that of the necessity for Senate reform.
Now, does that arise without any reason for it whatever? Of course it does not. As I said a moment ago, I propose to put on the record some of the wise and weighty sayings of the past, hoping that my words may find some target; if not here, they may find a target elsewhere. It is our manifest duty as servants of the public to try to carry this question to the bar of public opinion, and that is what I am trying to do. I repeat, I do not hope to make an impression on the government. They are not much inclined to take part in debate and are more likely to reply by saying "Didn't we win the last election?" They did win the last election in a big way, but if the result of that is that we are drifting into
5354	HOUSE OF
Proposed Senate Reform a situation where the House of Commons is no longer to be a debating institution, and where the government just waits until we are through and then votes, all I can say is that a House of Commons of that kind will not maintain a healthy existence for very long.
Reference has been made to the former prime minister and his attitude on the matter.
I propose to say very little about that. As a matter of fact there is at least this to be said. He showed some sense of humour about the matter. I never thought a sense of humour was his distinguishing quality, but he did say two things which struck me as rather humorous. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar some years ago asked him what consideration he was giving to this question, and as I recall it he said he had been considering it all his life. On another occasion in answer to a question by the late Miss Mac-phail, who was cross-examining him about improving the Senate, he said he was improving it; as fast as Conservatives died he was appointing Liberals in their place. I give him credit for that as a somewhat humorous remark.
His attitude otherwise on that matter we have had described tonight already. I say no more about it. The attitude of the present Prime Minister is something I am utterly unable to understand. I am sorry he is not here to hear what I am saying. I have not the exact words, but my understanding is that on a certain occasion within the last few months he said there were more important things to do, or words to that effect, than bother about the Senate. The impression left in my mind was that, in effect he said the public of Canada should not bother him about that matter because it was not of sufficient importance. If anyone wishes to correct my impression I would be glad to be corrected right now.

I do not think that is what the Prime Minister said. I am relying on my memory of what was said earlier. I believe he said he had not yet seen any scheme of reform that would be better than the status quo. That is what I would call a rather good Conservative position.

I shall pursue this matter, because I feel the minister has softened up the Prime Minister's remark a great deal. However, accepting it as he said it, then I am thrown back on a cynical interpretation which I do not want to accept; that is, that the remark seems to imply no desire to change a situation which contains so many useful plums. I hope that is not so; I do not want to think it is so.
All I can say is that if the Prime Minister believes the present situation of the Senate 

is satisfactory, I would think he is in a very small minority. I shall have occasion to say later that I do not believe either the Prime Minister or anyone in this house has reached such a stage of ineptitude that he feels when there is a problem to be solved we have to sit down and say nothing can be done about it. I feel that is not an attitude the Prime Minister would wish to put before us.
Now I wish to read certain quotations which I am taking from Professor MacKay's book. I feel it is desirable, first of all, that we try to take a square look at ourselves in this chamber, and second I think it is desirable that the public should have brought to their attention the views which have been held by people of experience who are entitled to have opinions on this matter. I propose to read first of all an extract from page 197, a quotation from Lord Bryce. I wish to stress the fact that Lord Bryce was, for several parliaments, a member of the British parliament before he became an ambassador. We all remember the extraordinary skill and discernment with which he wrote about the United States constitution, teaching them things they had never known before about their own affairs. I read his words, therefore, with great respect and I pass them on in the same way. Professor MacKay said:
A no less enthusiastic supporter of popular government than Lord Bryce was led to admit, at the close of a life of study and observation of representative institutions, that there were serious weaknesses apparently inherent in representative government. His conclusions were as follows:
"Legislatures contain too little of the stores of knowledge, wisdom, and experience which each country possesses.
"Legislatures are liable to fall under the control of one political party disposed to press through, in a hasty or tyrannical spirit, measures conceived in the interests of that party or of a particular class in the community, often without allowing sufficient time for full debate, sometimes even by means of an organization of the ruling majority which binds all its members to support whatever measures have been adopted by the larger part of that majority. Where this happens it is not the legislature as a whole that governs, but a majority of a majority which may frequently be a minority of the whole body . . .
I would think any man in this house would realize that we know of a legislature not very far away of which that is true. Further he says:
"It has begun to be perceived that the existing legislative machinery of most countries does not sufficiently provide for the study of economic and social problems in a directly practical spirit by those on whom the duty falls of passing into law measures dealing with them, because legislatures incessantly occupied with party strife and with the supervision of the executive in its daily work of administration have not the time, even if a sufficient number of their members have the capacity, for such investigation."
He goes on to speak in the same way. I want next to quote briefly from Sir John

Macdonald, then from George Brown and then from Cartier. From Macdonald I wish to quote this, taking it from page 37 of Mac-Kay's book. He is reporting on the Quebec conference, and I read first of all MacKay's comment:
The Question shifted, therefore, to the construction of the upper house. The importance of this question in the minds of the statesmen at Quebec may be gleaned from the fact that practically the whole of six days out of a total of 14 spent in discussing the details of the scheme were given over to the problem of constituting the second chamber. Here, as at Philadelphia, the particularism and the fears of the smaller provinces lay at the basis of the difficulties.
Here are Macdonald's words:
Now as to the constitution of the legislature we should have two chambers, an upper and a lower house. In the upper house equality in numbers should be the basis, in the lower house population should be the basis.
Then later on George Brown said, speaking of the upper house, that it was the key to federation, the very essence of the compact. He said:
Our Lower Canadian friends have agreed to give us representation by population in the lower house, on the express condition that they could have equality in the upper house. On no other condition could we have advanced a step.
Now I wish to quote from page 49 of this book, from Cartier:
The weak point in democratic institutions is the leaving of all power in the hands of the popular element. The history of the past proves this to be an evil. In order that institutions may be stable and work harmoniously there must be a power of resistance to oppose the democratic element.
I suppose if he had expanded that he would have made it clear that what he was talking about was the democratic element in headlong action and without any brake of any kind. Macdonald at the same time said:
There would be no use of an upper house if it did not exercise, when it thought proper, the right of opposing or amending or postponing the legislation of the lower house. It would be no value whatever were it a mere chamber for registering the decrees of the lower house. It must be an independent house, having a free action of its own, for it is only valuable as being a regulating body, calmly considering the legislation initiated by the popular branch, and preventing any hasty or ill-considered legislation which may come from that body.
In view of all the good work we admit the Senate has done I would like to ask why it has become, as one so often hears in conversation, a kind of butt. It never should have become a butt. I am not going to enlarge on its disabilities, which have been mentioned, but I will say that I think one of the reasons it has fallen from its high estate has been the attitude of the last prime minister and the present one. Their
Proposed Senate Reform views come to be known, and their views naturally affect the views of those who are about them. As a result, if those who are closest to the Senate adopt that attitude, then it is easy for it to spread.
I wish now to spend a few moments coming back to what I think was the last great period of the Senate, that between 1930 and 1935, when it was led by two distinguished men, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen and Senator Dandurand. I wish to quote from both of them but particularly from Senator Dandurand, to show some of the achievements of the Senate at that time, and the attitude of these men who were its leaders. This will give some indication of how very valuable the Senate has been and could be again. I think I have remarked in the house before that a friend of mine, who spent a good deal of time in Ottawa at that time, was tremendously impressed by the Senate. Indeed he said he was in favour of a singlechamber government, and would abolish the House of Commons. But, speaking seriously, I wish to quote now from Senator Dandurand.
What were the dates the hon. member just gave?
Between 1930 and 1935.
I think both those gentlemen led the Senate until about 1940 or 1941.

Perhaps it would have been more accurate if I had said that. However, I thought of those dates because the speeches I am about to read were delivered in 1932. I am ready to accept the hon. member's correction. I did not know whether Senator Dandurand had been there as late as 1940, and that was the reason I gave the dates I did.
The attitude of the House of Commons was different after that; that is, between 1935 and 1940.

I quote now the words of Senator Dandurand as they appear at page 7 of the debates of the Senate, in the session of 1932. Right Hon. Mr. Meighen had just joined the Senate and Senator Dandurand, in greeting him, said:
My right hon. friend will quickly observe there is really no opposition here; there is no standing opposition to government measures.
Bear in mind that he was leader of the opposition in the Senate.
In other words, we are collaborators in the work of the Senate, and we are that by reason of the fact that we are appointed for life, are independent of the electors, and have not to consider any constituency as a special unit from which we hold a mandate. Unlike the members in another place, we do not address the electors; we are content to address ourselves to the question-which is

Proposed Senate Reform
much the briefer way. Long speeches, such as may protract the debate in the popular house, are not made here.
Later on, speaking of one or two of the achievements of the Senate, he said:
To enumerate some of the measures that have passed under review in the Senate, I would mention the Railway Act, the Insurance Act, the Companies Act, the Bankruptcy Act and the Bank Act. I remember the revision of the Railway Act. The bill remained in our committee for weeks, and when it was returned to the House of Commons it contained seventy-two amendments. The Minister of Railways and the Minister of Justice, after thoroughly examining those amendments, accepted sixty-eight of them, and at a conference between the two houses as to retaining the others, my hon. friend from De Salaberry (Hon. Mr. Beique) was able to show the delegation from the other chamber that our amendments were proper ones and they were incorporated in the act.
Later he referred to the Insurance Act and the contribution made in that connection by the Senate.
Then I should like to read from the speech delivered on the same day by Mr. Meighen in which he said:
The honourable senator from De Lorimier (Mr. Dandurand) has dealt concisely, but in a way which to me has been illuminating, with the nature and function of this chamber as distinguished from the other, from which many of us have come. I take no exception at all to the distinction which he draws. I hope that the atmosphere of the other chamber does not too closely pursue us, and I promise honourable gentlemen opposite that I will make an honest effort to escape from that atmosphere and to acquire, even more than in the past, the habit of addressing myself to the question instead of to the public at large. Indeed, I thank the hon. member from De Lorimier for giving me tonight for the first time an explanation of the unfortunate fact that my public life to date has not been an unbroken and unqualified success.
What year was that?

1932. He continued:
It occurred to me as he spoke that in the other chamber I had been addicted too much to the practice of addressing myself to the question instead of to the public, and that the palm of victory finally went to those who addressed themselves to the public instead of to the issue.
I have read this, as I said, because I wish to put on record some indication of the standing the Senate had at that time. I can only hope, as I say, that my words may reach a target; and if I can make a contribution, even a small one, to an understanding and appreciation of the true seriousness of this situation I shall be perfectly content to have wearied the house, as I am doing.
As I have said, we see a very disappointing attitude in the House of Commons. In my view the Prime Minister is not taking the matter seriously, and has not given us the lead we should have. And when the Prime Minister does not give the lead it is hard for others to follow. I was amazed the other day when the Prime Minister spoke about there being a good many debates he did not like,

including the one we were prosecuting at that time. I could not help thinking that it was a strange thing to have a leader in a democratic assembly who did not like debating, because I have always believed that debating was the lifeblood of a democratic assembly; and that if it ceased, or became flat and ineffective, any democratic assembly would wither away.
He did not like the whole level of debate.

Well, it is hard to have a debate when it is all on one side. It would be better if the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) would take part in it. But this business of punching a rubber ball becomes tiresome at times.
You could always stop.

I am not going to suggest methods of reforming the Senate, because I think it would be a waste of time to start talking about those methods of reform until we have made up our minds that we want to do it, and that has not happened yet. I am addressing myself entirely to the idea of doing whatever minute part is in my power to spread the idea that what we need is a new attitude from the Prime Minister down.
Of course we could have a Senate in which we would have representatives who, as time went on, would command the ultimate respect of the public. There would be representatives first of politics, of course, because the Senate will always need people who are trained in politics. Then, second, there should be representatives trained in labour matters. Then, third-and some sceptics may question this- there should be representatives trained in the legal profession, others trained in engineering and in finance; all kinds of professions.
I am not going to suggest at the moment how they should be chosen. But I say again that if there were a will to do it, a way could be found quite easily. Or, to use the old music hall catch phrase, if there's a will there are three ways. It would not be difficult if it were desired. The plain fact is that it is not desired at the moment; it is not felt that it is worth while making an effort.
I think I shall forgo some further remarks I intended to make, Mr. Speaker. I want to repeat myself to this extent. I greatly regret that this question is not taken seriously by the government. We are entitled to make that remark when they refuse to take part in the debate. We had one interesting comment tonight by the Prime Minister, who cleared our minds on one point; but I maintain again that this is an important matter. I maintain that it is an entire dereliction of duty when the government refuse to take part in a

debate on this subject. I can only hope that as time goes on we may possibly be able to carry this to the court of public opinion. We have had some small success in doing that in another debate, perhaps more than we could have hoped, and I hope that in this matter, too, we shall continue to debate it again, again and again until the government are forced to recognize that it is an important matter which cannot be shrugged off, but which demands the best attention they can give it.
They have appointed a royal commission to advise them on economic matters. Why is it that a matter of this kind, which perhaps is even more important or just as important, is left disregarded, and in the meantime becomes almost a mockery to the public so that this honourable and serious institution is degraded in public opinion in a way which is utterly unfair to them and injurious to the public welfare?
(Translation) :

Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring my modest contribution to this debate, the purpose of which is to ask the government to implement a long overdue Senate reform.
First of all, let me congratulate the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) for his timely remarks, as well as all those who made suggestions.
Mr. Speaker, the Senate, where 22 seats are vacant-some have been unoccupied for five years-can surely not efficiently fulfil the task assigned to it. Since there are now only seven members of the political party to which I belong, the Senate is made up almost exclusively of members of the same party, and can no longer be considered a democratic institution.
Those vacancies should be filled with the least possible delay in order to restore to the Senate the prestige it had acquired in the past, but which has greatly decreased and even tends to disappear completely.
The public is inclined to believe that all the hon. senators have to do is to deal with the applications for divorce, which come up each year and are nearly all granted.
I refuse to believe that no more serious and practical work can be found for our senators to do than to give assent to the disruption of families and to approve shameful concubinage.
That should not be the function of the hon. members of the Senate. How can they do much more than study 400 divorce bills in a session,-a number which includes only the applications for divorce from the prov-
Proposed Senate Reform inces of Quebec and Newfoundland,-considering the small number of sitting days and the shortness of each sitting?
More importance should be attached to the Senate, which, by the way, occupies half of this building.
It is not the first time that Senate reform has come up for debate in this house.
The opposition has demanded such a reform more than once in the days of the late Mr. Mackenzie King, but Mr. King was not interested. He was only interested in appointing his own creatures after making especially sure that all would approve legislation submitted to them after its approval by this house.
I will only take a few minutes to reiterate a suggestion which I have already made at a meeting held in my constituency on October 14, 1954.
While advocating Senate reform, on that occasion, I suggested that the provinces ought to have a say in the appointment of senators. This, to my mind, would be far more in line with the intentions of the fathers of confederation, all due account being taken, of course, of de facto changes introduced in the meantime.
The fate and future of the provinces being at stake, because of the ever-spreading centralization of the federal government, it is more than ever expedient, if we sincerely want provincial governments to survive, to give to the so-called Senate the character of defender of the threatened rights of the provinces, by allowing the provinces to appoint a large proportion of its members.
The province of Quebec includes nearly a third of the population of Canada and the few senators representing that largest minority group of the country do not reflect the public opinion of that province, especially as their past political allegiance is far too much in agreement with that of the government which has held power now for over 20 years.
They are therefore not in a position to reflect the opinions of the people of Quebec, since they are opposed to those opinions, as represented by the present provincial government elected by the people, and even fight those opinions.
Once again, I make a claim for the respect due to the province of Quebec. It would be paying due respect to that province to allow it to appoint to the Senate men in whom it has complete faith, who would speak on behalf of its people but above all would be the champions of their most sacred rights.
If the party now in office does not want the Senate to lose its character of a federal body, it is only fair that it should add to the sena-
