Proposed Senate Reform, tors appointed by it a certain number of other people who would be appointed by the provincial governments and, when opportunity affords, could make their voices heard.
Filling the Senate vacancies according to the importance of the two majority groups of population in this country and having regard to the rights of the provinces is the bounden duty of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) himself. I urge him therefore to discharge that duty as soon as possible in order to restore the standard of prestige to which the Senate is rightfully entitled.
I also urge the Prime Minister, in the name of millions of Canadian workers to whom we owe our economic development, to appoint at least one of them to that important post.
Such an appointment would be a tribute to the worker, to his character, to his ability as well as to the large contribution he makes daily to the development of our country.
I know that such a request has been made many times in the past andi, representing as I do a county practically all made up of workers, I venture to speak in the name of these worthy workers in order that they may be represented in the Canadian Senate by at least one of their own.
As I was saying a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time the question of Senate reform is raised in this parliament. The question has been broached a great many times not only here but everywhere in Canada. Should we not follow for once the example given by various other commonwealth countries which have adopted various reforms with respect to their upper chamber? The new Prime Minister of England, Sir Anthony Eden, has recognized, since he came to power, that it is necessary to proceed with a reform of the House of Lords-the equivalent of the Canadian Senate-and a committee has already been established and given the task of studying the possibility of applying the appropriate reforms.
New Zealand, another great commonwealth country, has definitely decided for the abolition of the Senate. In Australia, a reform was necessary and it was brought about.
I therefore say it is time we should follow the example of other countries as important as ours, that we should follow the example even of the mother country, so that the Canadian Senate may undergo the necessary reform.
We never had in Canada a more inefficient upper house; there is none like it in the whole world.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member is going a little too far, when he contends that the upper house is the most inefficient in the world. According to the practice and standing order number 41, we must not here in this house attack either individually or as a whole the members of the upper house. And, even if several perhaps derogatory expressions have been allowed, I believe, however, that the hon. member might better keep within reasonable bounds.
Mr. Speaker, maybe it was a slip of the tongue, because nothing was further from my mind-
A calculated one.

-and I had no intention to attack the hon. members of the Senate. I only want to say, as I said before, that the Canadian upper house cannot be effective in view of the fact that, first of all, the long-expected reform did not take place, and also, more particularly, because the Senate is lacking 22 members.
Mr. Speaker, if you do not have any objections, and as it is now ten o'clock, I shall move the adjournment of the debate.
No. There are two more minutes. Go on.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Apparently the hon. member has not the unanimous consent of the house at this time to have it called six o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, in order to be able to prove some of my contentions, and to show the extent to which that honourable house could be more effective, if a reform were granted by the government in power, I would like to tell the house about an editorial published in the Montreal Gazette of February 3, 1954, from which I shall quote.
It will take about five minutes, Mr. Speaker. (Text):
It is entitled "The Forsaken Garden". Somebody has called it ten o'clock.
